entries.title: With closer Daniel Palencia on IL, denizens of Cubs’ bullpen ‘dungeon’ have thrived in ninth inning
entries.summary: <p>BALTIMORE — What sort of pitchers are the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> trusting to close out games these days?</p><p>Dungeon-dwellers.</p><p>“It’s a weird vibe,” lefty reliever Ryan Rolison said of the underneath-the-bleachers Wrigley Field bullpen. “A lot of us want to be able to experience the crowd at Wrigley and to be able to soak in the atmosphere.</p><p>“But we’ve got to create that on our own down there in the dungeon.”</p><p>The sunshine and fresh air Ernie Banks immortalized? These pitchers don’t see it and don’t breathe it.</p><p>“We’ve got the Plexiglas up, so we can’t really hear the crowd that well,” Rolison said. “There’s chaos going on around us, and it’s just quiet in that dungeon.”</p><p>But the seas have been anything but quiet for the relief corps of late, with a roster’s worth of arms on the injured list simultaneously.</p><p>There’s no bigger sidelined name than righty Daniel Palencia, the fireballing closer who’s been down since June 16 working back from an inflamed elbow.</p><p>While injuries to righties Phil Maton, Hunter Harvey, Porter Hodge and Ethan Roberts, along with lefty Hoby Milner, have generated needs throughout the late innings, the Cubs have had to turn to a host of arms to try to get the game’s final three outs.</p><p>And they’ve done it with great success.</p><p>Coming into Wednesday, Cubs relievers boasted a 2.12 ninth-inning ERA since June 16 that ranked seventh in baseball.</p><p>Overall, results have been mixed. Since that June 16 date, the bullpen as a whole has an ERA above 5.00.</p><p>But the ninth-inning numbers are strong, and given the unexpected arms that are being deployed with games on the line, the frequency of big performances has been impressive.</p><p>“There were a bunch of injuries, and a bunch of us new faces got an opportunity,” Rolison said. “It’s a testament to everyone being ready when their name’s called.”</p><p>“I haven’t really ever pitched in leverage situations, so being able to have the opportunity to do that is great. Once you see you have success in leverage spots like that, it helps the confidence. I’ve seen myself be successful in those situations, and it helps me a lot as a pitcher to have experience like that.”</p><p>Rolison’s just one of a dozen arms to pitch in the ninth since Palencia went down, one of 10 to not give up a run in the ninth; only righties Jacob Webb and Jayden Murray have been scored on.</p><p>Webb has been tapped more than anyone, pitching the ninth in five games. He was scored upon in his first two outings after Palencia’s injury, but only one of those came in the ninth inning. Since, Webb has a six-outing scoreless streak.</p><p>The late-inning group includes somewhat unlikely names like Rolison, Webb and righties Trent Thornton and Tyler Ferguson, the guys manager Craig Counsell has at his disposal while others heal.</p><p>“We’re just trying to match it up and get guys in the right spots as best we can, knowing that [opposing teams are] going to unload benches, at times,” Counsell said Tuesday. “They’ve done great.”</p><p>That’s life in the bullpen, with all the mixing and matching meaning pitchers are told which parts of lineups they’ll face rather than which inning they can expect to pitch in.</p><p>And there’s been a lot of movement, too. With all the injuries, the bullpen is currently far from how Jed Hoyer’s front office drew it up. But the Cubs traded for Ferguson in May, traded for Murray in June, picked righty Bryse Wilson up off the waiver wire and brought lefty Drew Pomeranz back on a minor league deal.</p><p>“It feels a little weird, like I didn’t leave,” said Pomeranz, who pitched in six Cubs playoff games last season. “It feels like I picked right back up where I left off, to be honest.</p><p>“Last year was a special year for me, playing in Chicago, playing at Wrigley, playing for the Cubs. It’s easy to be excited about that every day.”</p><p>With ninth-inning results like these, what’s not to be excited about?</p><p>Even when you’re living in a dungeon.</p><bsp-listcarousel entries.title: Man fatally shot by several attackers in Woodlawn
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot by a group of people in Woodlawn Wednesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 34, was standing outside in the 6700 block of South Cottage Grove Avenue at 7:20 p.m. when people exited two SUVs, one gray and one white, and began firing in his direction, police said. He was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center, where he died.</p><p>No one is in custody.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: What time is Cubs' game with Orioles? Forecasted rain moves series finale to afternoon in Baltimore
entries.summary: <p>BALTIMORE – The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> and Orioles will play a matinee with rain in the forecast Thursday night in Maryland.</p><p>An ugly outlook for baseball forced a change from a night game to an afternoon start, with first pitch moving from 5:35 p.m. Central to 12:35 p.m. Central.</p><p>The two teams <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/07/cubs-rain-delay-orioles-camden-yards-weather-baltimore-first-pitch" >sat through a nearly hourlong delay</a> before the start of the first game of this three-game series Tuesday night.</p><p>The Cubs will go for a three-game sweep of the Orioles on Thursday after taking the first two games in the series.<br></p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: White Sox scouting head Mike Shirley says team wants best player in draft, regardless of money — to a point
entries.summary: <p>No one knows whom the White Sox will take with the first pick in the MLB Draft on Saturday. And according to Sox director of amateur scouting Mike Shirley, that includes the Sox.</p><p>“I don’t know who it is yet,” Shirley said Wednesday. “That’s the best part. And I feel like we’re going to keep working up to the moment to figure that out.”</p><p>We do know this: Shirley said the Sox have narrowed their choices to shortstops Roch Cholowsky and Grady Emerson and catcher Vahn Lackey, though it’s widely believed the pick will come down to the two shortstops.</p><p>When the Sox won the draft lottery in December, UCLA’s Cholowsky was considered the top player on the board. Since then, Emerson, a high school player out of Fort Worth (Texas) Christian, has made the pick a toss-up. Georgia Tech’s Lackey adds to the intrigue.</p><p>We also know that under the direction of general manager Chris Getz, the Sox won’t select a player based on needs in the majors or the farm system. And money won’t be an issue, either — to a point.</p><p>“He’s told us we’re taking the best player,” Shirley said. “It’s not about the major-league team, it’s not about the money; it’s about who is the best player. It’s a little bit out of our hands if the representation of the player asks for a record bonus that we’re not comfortable with. That would be the only indication that may make us pivot, what the actual costs were.”</p><p>Those could be interesting conversations, especially considering Cholowsky and Emerson have the same representation. Perhaps that’s why Lackey is still in the mix.</p><p>Nevertheless, the Sox will come away with a premium player at a position they covet. Getz has said it’s no coincidence they prefer shortstops — they’re generally the best players on their teams. Three of the Sox’ last five first-round picks have been shortstops. And quality catchers are hard to find, as the major-league team has experienced this season.</p><p>Shirley is keenly aware of Cholowsky’s abilities, having scouting him when Cholowsky was in high school.</p><p>“You see a much stronger player; he’s more physically advanced,” he said. “He is foundational on the field with his habits, he’s a leader on the field, he has a very secure defense at shortstop. I think the power is real.”</p><p>Emerson has been coached in high school by former major-leaguer Rusty Greer.</p><p>“Anytime you’re around someone at the major-league level, they’re going to support you like that,” Shirley said. “Grady’s an elite high school player. [He has] an elite high school hit tool, and he does it really easy. So we’re zeroing in on these guys pretty good.</p><p>“And even Vahn Lackey is a supreme athlete who really could define the catching position and be foundational defensively. There’s a lot of traits to him that we’re continuing to dig in.”</p><p>Shirley isn’t worried about the time a high school player might need to develop, as evidenced by the Sox’ first-round pick last year, high school shortstop Billy Carlson, whom MLB.com ranks as the fourth-best prospect in their system.</p><p>“High school players are facing 95 [mph], they’re facing 98,” Shirley said. “They’re accustomed to the stuff. So it’s not like when they get to the major leagues, it’s going to be the first time they ever see that.</p><p>“It’s not about what they are today; it’s about what they’re going to be two to three years from now when they show up here at the major-league level.”</p><p>And Shirley doesn’t want to be picking first overall two to three years from now — or ever again.</p><p>“I want to pass this on to someone else, and I want the White Sox to win a championship real soon,” he said. “I don’t want to lose the way we lost to get here; that was painful. But how can you not be excited to have the No. 1 pick and with the direction of the club?</p><h3><b>MLB DRAFT</b></h3><p>Noon Saturday, Picks 1-10, NBC 5</p><p>1:30 p.m., Picks 11-40, MLB</p><div entries.title: Chicago Public Library Foundation names new CEO
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Public Library Foundation has named a new CEO Wednesday, five months after the death of its former leader.</p><p>The foundation, which raises private funds for numerous programs and activities at city libraries, appointed Eva Giglio.</p><p>Giglio previously worked as a middle and high school Spanish teacher at Kenwood Academy. She later served as a deputy chief of staff under former Chicago Public Schools CEO Janice K. Jackson, where she helped lead the district's five-year strategic plan and worked to safely reopen schools during the pandemic.</p><p>Most recently, she has worked as the executive director of the CME Group Foundation, one of Chicago’s leading education funders, where she directed an annual grantmaking budget of $6.7 million.</p><p>Giglio, who will begin her new job in August, was selected from more than 100 applicants.</p><p>"Early in the process, Eva stood out because of her strategic thinking, warm personality, and deep network," said Michael Fassnacht, chair of the library foundation’s board. "She knows business leaders and education leaders and just understands and knows and loves Chicago."</p><p>She will take over the foundation five months after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/02/03/brenda-langstraat-bui-ceo-of-chicago-public-library-foundation-dies-at-52" >the death of its previous CEO, Brenda Langstraat Bui,</a> who died following a tragic accident at her home in the West Loop. She was 52.</p><p>"I knew Brenda," said Giglio. "I feel it's such an honor to carry on her legacy."</p><p>Giglio, 39, grew up in Rogers Park before moving to Glenview as a kid. She attended Glenbrook South High School before studying teaching and Spanish at the University of Illinois. She lived in the city for many years before moving back to Glenview for family reasons.</p><p>Giglio, a mother of three who enjoys competing in triathlons in her spare time, plans to hit the ground running in August by working with the Chicago Public Library on a number of initiatives, including making sure the city's public libraries offer a pathway for people to learn about and use artificial intelligence.</p><p>She also plans to focus on literacy. "We need a citywide strategy to improve growth and proficiency," she said.</p><p>She also loves to read. She's currently reading "Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow" — a work of fiction about two childhood friends who become creative partners in the video game industry. </p><p>She's also reading "James and the Giant Peach" to her eight-year-old daughter.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox prospect Caleb Bonemer credits added strength for production at plate
entries.summary: <p>Chicago is becoming overwhelmed with Calebs. The Bears have Caleb Williams, and the Bulls have Caleb Wilson. In a year or two, the White Sox might have Caleb Bonemer.</p><p>He’ll represent the Sox in the All-Star Futures Game on Sunday in Philadelphia. The 20-year-old infielder is the Sox’ top-ranked prospect, according to MLB.com. The club promoted him to Double-A Birmingham last month, and he continues to produce at the plate, posting a .772 OPS with three home runs in 18 games.</p><p>“My strength as a hitter is pulling the baseball in the air,” Bonemer said Wednesday. “This year, I’ve been able to hit a few homers. That’s definitely been my strong suit. I think when I’m going well, I can hit for average and hit for power. My strength this year has been the slugging; homers, extra-base hits.”</p><p>That came after he added strength on the recommendation of Sox director of hitting Ryan Fuller.</p><p>“This year, I got a little bit bigger,” said Bonemer, who’s listed at 6-1, 195 pounds. “Some of my homers, I kind of mis-hit balls, and I’m stronger so they’re able to go out. I just try to be a complete hitter, and then the homers will come.”</p><p>They sure came at High-A Winston-Salem, where Bonemer hit 18 in 61 games this season with a .937 OPS before being promoted.</p><p>“It’s gone pretty good so far,” he said of his time in Birmingham. “Just trying to repeat what I’ve been doing. I’m not really trying to change a whole lot. Even if I have a rough game, just still trying to go out there and do what I know works.”</p><p>Maybe having another Caleb in town will work. Asked if he’s aware of the trend, Bonemer replied, “I know Caleb Williams.”</p><p>It’s a start.</p><h3>Hitters have no answer in shutout</h3><p>The Red Sox held the White Sox to four hits again, but this time they kept them off the scoreboard in a 5-0 victory. The White Sox hadn’t been shut out at home since Aug. 13, 2025, in a 1-0 loss to the Tigers.</p><p>“Another tough game,” manager Will Venable said. “Really credit to another really good lefty with a really good fastball. We’ve seen a lot of foul balls on fastballs in the zone; just haven’t been able to get on top of them and hit them hard. A lot like [Tuesday].”</p><p>Venable said Red Sox starter Jake Bennett, like Payton Tolle before him, fooled White Sox hitters with his extension. The 6-6, 234-pounder allowed four hits with one walk in seven innings.</p><p>“They’re getting on these guys really fast,” Venable said. “You really have to be ready early and find solutions to get on top and move them forward. These guys trained all day to be ready for those fastballs, and sometimes you have to give the other guy credit.”</p><p>“I think that was the best located game by a starter against us all season,” Randal Grichuk said. “Got to tip your cap some nights.”</p><p>Davis Martin struggled again, allowing five runs and six hits in four innings. Last Thursday, he allowed two runs, six hits and five walks in only 3 ⅓ innings.</p><h3>Murakami update</h3><p>Munetaka Murakami came out unscathed from his first rehab game Tuesday for Charlotte. On Wednesday, he had an RBI double in his first at-bat — with an exit velocity of 101.4 mph — and later walked and scored while playing first base for the entire game.</p><p>“Good reports that he recovered well, came out of it nicely,” Venable said of Murakami’s first game, “and obviously a good job in the field.”</p><p>Whether two games are enough for Murakami and the Sox remains to be seen. Both are taking it day by day. Venable has said Murakami might need only a couple of games before returning. That could happen Friday, which would mark six weeks since he strained his right hamstring.</p><h3>Another start for Junior</h3><p>White Sox rookie outfielder Junior Perez got consecutive starts for only the second time this season, thanks to the Red Sox starting left-handers on consecutive days. He has played in only 14 games since being called up June 18, but he has Venable’s support.</p><p>“Really good tool set where he’s playing above-average defense at multiple positions,” Venable said. “He can run, he can throw, really a good swing-decision guy. We’ve seen the power.</p><p>“The way that he is in the clubhouse, the way that he’s engaging with our coaches, there’s a ton of aptitude there, where he’s making adjustments and doing everything he can to get better. Real big fan of JP.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" entries.title: A simultaneous, worldwide reading of the Declaration of Independence draws 'hopeful' crowd in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>A desire to celebrate America’s 250th birthday brought two former history majors to Newberry Library for a live reading of the Declaration of Independence on Wednesday.</p><p>Though nearly 40 years apart, the two women expressed a common goal to be optimistic amid the country’s shortcomings.</p><p>“We’re a beacon for the world — hopefully — still,” said Ellyn Robinson, 61, of the Gold Coast. "There's some things that have changed in the last couple years, but I am hopeful.<b> </b>I am hopeful. We've had this great experiment that's been tested in lots of generations, and now we're facing our test in our generation to prove ourselves worthy of the Declaration and the Constitution that were left for us.”</p><p>Isabella Barboza, 22, who lives in East Side, said she also finds the Declaration of Independence meaningful, even though she views it as more of an “ideal” than a reality.</p><p>“Not everyone in the United States is treated equally,” said Barboza, who recently graduated from Yale. “I think it’s nice to aspire to that, and that's why I came.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/things-to-do/2026/07/01/america-250-july-4-weekend-chicago-events-declaration-independence" >America’s 250th birthday has arrived. the Declaration of Independence at 5 p.m. in Chicago; in all, it was read in more than <a class="Link" href="https://hawaiiamerica250.org/reading-locations" target="_blank" ><u>1,000 locations</u></a>. Sponsored by the <a class="Link" href="https://hawaiiamerica250.org/sharing-the-spirit-of-america" target="_blank" ><u>Hawai’i America250 Commission</u></a>, the event commemorated America’s 250th anniversary and the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nps.gov/inde/learn/news/first-public-reading-of-the-declaration-of-independence.htm" target="_blank" ><u>first public reading of the document</u></a> in Philadelphia on July 8, 1776. In Illinois, participants included the American Writers Museum, Pullman National Historical Park and <a class="Link" href="https://www.il250.org/declaration?fbclid=IwY2xjawS7TyRleHRuA2FlbQIxMABicmlkETEwSGNZYk9mYTU1aFJZSXJqc3J0YwZhcHBfaWQQMjIyMDM5MTc4ODIwMDg5MgABHoJfGtYxkzvzbzLjeX_KeegF4LvxPdDFcIpfoiaodC52EEwZ1u_wLhWereeR_aem_wJ-JRBLORG4PK5xIJUYbZg" target="_blank" ><u>dozens of other cultural organizations, courthouses and sites</u></a>.</p><p>Newberry Library attendees read the text aloud from pocket-sized booklets distributed statewide by the Illinois America 250 Commission, which encouraged reflection on the promise of equal rights for all, a government that answers to the people, and Illinois’ role in the story of America. They also perused the library’s current exhibit, “Free and Independent: The Declaration of Independence and the Words That Made the United States.” The exhibit includes a rare, early copy of the document. Overall, the event fostered strong feelings of patriotism, camaraderie and contemplation.</p><p>“There's so much going on right now, and it feels very poignant to take this time to come together in these kinds of public spaces and share in what it all means,” said Jill Austin, Newberry Library’s vice president for public engagement. “There is a lot for us all to reflect on — to think about how we got here and what role we all have to play in the present in order to ensure a more perfect future for the next generations.”</p><p>The reading was kicked off by “Free and Independent” exhibit curator Eric Slauter, who is also deputy dean of the Humanities Division at the University of Chicago. The audience of mostly older Chicagoans took less than 15 minutes to read the approximately 1,300-word document.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: U.S. Attorney Boutros still due in court Thursday after failing to convince judge to cancel hearing
entries.summary: <p>Eighteen hours before he was due to appear in court, U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros<b> </b>tried to assure a magistrate judge Wednesday<b> </b>he didn’t mean to violate one of her orders by touting sealed criminal charges<b> </b>at a press conference with top Justice Department officials last week.</p><p>Boutros explained himself<b> </b>in a 14-page document<b> </b>filed<b> </b>Wednesday<b> </b>afternoon. And even though U.S. Magistrate Judge Laura<b> </b>McNally<b> </b>had<b> </b>ordered<b> </b>him<b> </b>to appear in court Thursday<b> </b>morning,<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>told the judge, “there is no need for a further hearing.”</p><p>McNally apparently disagreed. In an order entered a short time later,<b> </b>she told Boutros, “the motion is denied.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/03/judge-orders-u-s-attorney-boutros-into-court-over-potential-violations-of-seal-order" >Judge orders U.S. Attorney Boutros into court over ‘potential violations’ of seal order</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Now, court watchers are waiting to see if Chicago’s embattled top federal prosecutor will appear in court Thursday<b> </b>morning. The hearing is set to take place in the chief judge’s courtroom on the 25th floor of the Dirksen Federal Courthouse, one of the largest courtrooms in the building.</p><p>It all comes seven weeks<b> </b>into a credibility crisis for Boutros that began with the May 21 collapse of the<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six” prosecution</a> over apparent prosecutor misconduct. The damage has continued to spread, even to cases unrelated to the<b> </b>six Operation Midway Blitz protesters.</p><p>Boutros’ office raised eyebrows again Tuesday night when it formally acknowledged it would not fight a bid by members of the “Broadview Six”<b> </b>to have their attorneys’ fees paid.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Assistant U.S. Attorney Maxwell<b> </b>Lisy<b> </b>wrote in a court filing that the United States “does not concede that the United States has acted or done anything to warrant those fees.”<b> </b>Lisy also insisted no effort should be allowed to seek evidence of such wrongdoing.</p><p>Boutros dodged at least two other high-stakes hearings in recent weeks. U.S. District Judge Sharon Johnson Coleman<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" >threatened to hold a hearing</a><b> </b>in June over allegations of prosecutor misconduct that surfaced in a case over which she presides. Boutros avoided it by permanently dropping charges against two defendants.</p><p>Boutros’ office also recently convinced<b> </b>U.S. Magistrate Judge Keri<b> </b>Holleb<b> </b>Hotaling<b> </b>to hold off on a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/18/boutros-holleb-hotaling-atf-country-club-hills" target="_blank" >sanctions hearing<b> </b>aimed at the feds</a><b> </b>after a video<b> </b>raised questions<b> </b>about the accuracy of a sworn affidavit in another case.</p><p>Boutros’ team argued that Holleb Hotaling<b> </b>had no authority to hold the hearing. The judge agreed to a “brief”<b> </b>delay<b> </b>and sought input<b> </b>from defense attorneys.</p><p>Now, McNally has called a hearing<b> </b>over<b> </b>“potential violations”<b> </b>of<b> </b>her<b> </b>order<b> </b>sealing<b> </b>criminal charges against<b> </b>alleged<b> </b>Tren de Aragua<b> </b>gang<b> </b>members. Boutros discussed the case July 1 during a press conference with Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche<b> </b>and FBI Director Kash Patel.</p><p>McNally wrote on the court docket that prosecutors<b> </b>called<b> </b>her<b> </b>chambers<b> </b>at 10:05 a.m.<b> </b>the day of the press conference, seeking an order unsealing<b> </b>the criminal complaint, with certain redactions, claiming they<b> </b>"needed to obtain a ruling within the next 15 minutes.”</p><p>The judge did not agree to unseal the complaint until the next day.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A photo from the criminal complaint filed against Josue Pacheco Torres, Kleiver Monasterio Briceno and Julian Pachano. Authorities say it depicts — from left to right — the kidnap victim, Torres, and an unnamed co-conspirator. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>U.S. District Court</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Boutros<b> </b>wrote<b> </b>Wednesday<b> </b>that he acted in good faith<b> </b>and believed the press conference “complied with the letter and spirit of the sealing order”<b> </b>because it was for the purpose of “facilitating ‘the enforcement of criminal law.’”</p><p>McNally’s<b> </b>seal<b> </b>order<b> </b>did<b> </b>“not prohibit law enforcement personnel from disclosing” documents<b> </b>in the case “as necessary to facilitate the enforcement of criminal law,” he pointed out.</p><p>One purpose of the press conference was to “deter future crimes”<b> </b>by Tren de Aragua “by publicly demonstrating that federal law enforcement would prioritize the prosecution and punishment of violent offenses”<b> </b>they committed, Boutros argued.</p><p>“The U.S. Attorney reasonably believed that disclosure of the arrests and charges of [Tren de Aragua] members helped facilitate the government’s enforcement of criminal law both in and outside of this district,” he wrote.</p><p>Boutros is being closely watched as he navigates a scandal unlike any faced by his recent predecessors. A chorus of local Democratic elected officials has insisted on his resignation, and a resolution<b> </b>calling for him to step down<b> </b>is moving through the Chicago City Council.</p><p>Boutros’ office<b> </b>issued an unusual statement responding to that resolution Tuesday, suggesting an ulterior motive behind the criticism. It<b> </b>said<b> </b>his<b> </b>office<b> </b>would<b> </b>“not be bullied into dropping its public corruption matters or closing out its newly opened ones.”</p><p>“No one faces this level of coordinated opposition and performative theatrics unless they are viewed as representing an existential threat to a system that is largely corrupt and broken” the statement read.</p><p>It added, “when this sort of coordinated panic sets in, it means that our federal leaders are on to something big.”</p>

entries.title: Behind back-to-back 20-20 guy Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs flex power with early Home Run Derby
entries.summary: <p>BALTIMORE — Isn’t the Home Run Derby on Monday?</p><p>Forgive the confusion, what with the display the Cubs and Orioles put on Wednesday night at Camden Yards.</p><p>The teams combined to hit nine homers, putting on the type of show heading for Philadelphia next week. The Cubs, with five of those dingers, grabbed a 9-7 victory and won their fourth consecutive road series.</p><p><b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> kept doing All-Star things, homering twice and clinching a second straight season of at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">what's better than 20 home runs?<br>21 home runs. <a href="https://t.co/EIhTXcJWD1">pic.twitter.com/EIhTXcJWD1</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2075006505934274845?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 8, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><p>On brand for a guy who’s busy filling up the record book this summer, Crow-Armstrong became the third Cub ever with multiple 20-20 seasons, joining <b>Sammy Sosa</b> and <b>Ryne Sandberg</b>. He’s the first major leaguer since another former Cub, <b>Alfonso Soriano</b>, to hit the 20-20 benchmark in back-to-back seasons before the All-Star break; Soriano did it in 2002 and 2003 with the Yankees.</p><p>After a spectacular June that ranked as one of baseball’s all-time great months, Crow-Armstrong is sizzling to start July: batting .476 with three homers, six RBI, six runs scored and three walks in six games.</p><p>“It tells you the start that his career is off to,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said after Wednesday’s game. “It’s a young career, it’s brand new, but he’s doing things that the greats in the game have done.”</p><p>Outfielders <b>Michael Conforto</b> and <b>Seiya Suzuki</b> and catcher <b>Carson Kelly</b> also homered Wednesday, showing the power potential the Cubs have up and down the lineup, a helpful thing as they try to chase down the division-leading Brewers.</p><h3><b>Back this season?</b></h3><p>Lefty starter <b>Justin Steele</b> doesn’t figure to be a starter if he can make it back before the end of the campaign. That was the message from team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> last month, and the Cubs are hammering that point home as Steele continues to recover from the elbow surgery that knocked him out at the beginning of last season and the ensuing setback that’s delayed his return.</p><p>“The schedule is very tight with Justin, and it doesn’t leave for a lot of things to happen, there’s no question about it,” Counsell said. “Stretching out as a starter is really not realistic with the calendar.”</p><p>Time will tell if Steele, who Counsell said will begin throwing off a mound at the beginning of next month, can make it back to factor into the Cubs’ plans as a bullpen arm as they hope for an extended playoff run.</p><p>Then there’s <b>Hunter Harvey</b>, the righty reliever signed to a free-agent deal last winter. He made four appearances in the early days of the season before hitting the IL with triceps inflammation.</p><p>He’s said to be on a throwing program, but the clock is ticking when it comes to whether he can make an impact this season.</p><p>“He’s missed a lot of time. I think the concern is real,” Counsell said. “We haven’t been able to start something and keep going. At some point, we’re just going to have to do that and see where that gets us. And that’s what we’re doing right now.”</p><h3><b>Maton on the mend</b></h3><p>Injured reliever <b>Phil Maton</b>, who’s been sidelined with a knee injury since late last month, pitched as part of a minor league rehab assignment Wednesday, retiring all five batters he faced, with three strikeouts, in a game with Triple-A Iowa.</p><p>According to Counsell, the righty will make one more rehab appearance prior to the All-Star break and is expected to return to the big league club shortly after the break, should everything go well.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module entries.title: Cash App parent company agrees to $45 million settlement with Illinois, 44 other states
entries.summary: <p>Illinois will get $1.1 million of a $45 million, 45-state settlement with money transfer app Cash App’s parent company, which was accused of misleading customers about the app’s security.</p><p>Block Inc. will face $55 million in civil penalties and also have to pay customers nationwide somewhere from $75 million to $120 million as part of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.consumerfinance.gov/enforcement/actions/block-inc/" target="_blank" ><u>settlement</u></a>, which includes the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.</p><p>In a statement, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul said the settlement holds the company accountable and requires it to “change its harmful practices.”</p><p>“Block told Cash App users their money was safe and falsely implied that the app worked like a bank, with the same protections,” Raoul said. “Block was aware that fraud on its platform was rising sharply and failed to warn users, strengthen protections or provide real help to users when things went wrong.”</p><p>A company spokesperson confirmed the settlement and said the company has made "significant investments in consumer protection, customer service, and compliance." </p><p>"We share the commitment of the attorneys general to addressing industry challenges and continue to invest in operations and technology to promote a safe and healthy financial ecosystem," the spokesperson said in a statement provided to the Sun-Times Wednesday night.</p><p>The lawsuit accused the company of not preventing fraud, and even of having systems that made it easier to commit that fraud. Minimal identity verification allowed someone to create fake or multiple accounts, and the company had no phone support line. Instead, customers who had been defrauded often were provided by those fraudsters with fake online customer support phone numbers, the suit alleged.</p><p>As part of the agreement, the company must offer at least 13.5 hours of human-staffed phone lines per day as part of 24-hour support, as well as reimburse customers for fraudulent transactions, stop marketing the app as safe and educate users about the dangers of fraud.</p>

entries.title: Phil Regan, former MLB pitcher and coach who spent time with the Cubs and White Sox, dies at 89
entries.summary: <p>Phil Regan, who pitched for four major league teams — including the Cubs and White Sox — over 13 years before spending five more decades in the game as a coach, manager and scout, died on Wednesday. He was 89.</p><p>Regan died peacefully of natural causes, his attorney, Matthew Blit, told The Associated Press.</p><p>Nicknamed "The Vulture" by teammate Sandy Koufax for his penchant for well-timed entries from the bullpen that earned him 58 wins over 446 career relief appearances, Regan was named an All-Star in 1966 in his first season with the Los Angeles Dodgers as he went 14-1 with a 1.62 ERA in 65 games and a National League-most 21 saves.</p><p>Regan broke in with his home-state Detroit Tigers in 1960 and started 101 games over his first six years in the majors, before becoming a full-time reliever in the NL. The right-hander moved onto the Cubs in 1968 until a 10-game stint with the White Sox in 1972 to finish his final major league season. Regan went 96-81 with a 3.84 ERA over 551 games and 92 saves in his career, with an ERA more than a full run lower as a reliever (3.30) than a starter (4.44).</p><p>The native of Otsego, Michigan, made a bigger mark once he left the mound. He built a rich resume that included nine years as the head baseball coach at Grand Valley State University, more than two decades of managing in the Dominican and Venezuelan winter leagues, and one season as manager of the Baltimore Orioles in 1995. Regan was also the pitching coach for four different major league teams — Seattle, Cleveland, the Cubs and the New York Mets — and Team USA at the 2000 Sydney Olympics.</p><p>Regan succeeded Johnny Oates for the strike-shortened 1995 season with the Orioles, managing three future Hall of Fame players — Cal Ripken Jr., Mike Mussina and Harold Baines — while posting a 71-73 record. He was replaced by Davey Johnson after one year.</p><p>Lured out of retirement in 2009 by the Mets, Regan then spent seven years as pitching coach for Class A affiliate St. Lucie before moving into a role as minor league assistant pitching coordinator. He had a hand in the development of standouts like Jacob deGrom, Seth Lugo, Steven Matz, Paul Sewald and Noah Syndergaard as they moved through the farm system.</p><p>He was promoted to interim major league pitching coach midway through the 2019 season at age 82 to replace the fired Dave Eiland. After serving three more years with the organization as a senior adviser of pitching development, Regan sued the Mets and then-general manager Brodie Van Wagenen for age discrimination and wrongful termination. The Mets hired Jeremy Hefner, who was 33 at the time, for the pitching coach job in 2020.</p><p>Regan had four children with his first wife, Carol, who died in 2004. He met his second wife, Lissette, while coaching in Venezuela.</p><p>"His life was dedicated to the game and his family, especially the 18 grandkids that he just adored," Blit said. "There is so much about Phil here in the States, but what most people don't know about is his impact in Venezuela. He coached for many years there and had the respect of so many of the Venezuelan players. But he would always say that his greatest reward from coaching in Venezuela was his wife."<br></p>

entries.title: MLB Network leading production of NBC's MLB Draft, the first on broadcast TV
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox might have said they’ve narrowed their choices for the first pick in the MLB Draft to three. But MLB Network is pretty confident there are really two.</p><p>The network will have cameras with shortstops Roch Cholowsky of UCLA and Grady Emerson of Fort Worth (Texas) Christian High School to get either’s instant reaction when MLB commissioner Rob Manfred announces the pick Saturday in Philadelphia. Other prospects, such as catcher Vahn Lackey — whom the Sox included in their final three – will be available via Zoom.</p><p>That’s just part of the coverage MLB Network has planned for the draft, which will be baseball’s first on broadcast TV. NBC will carry MLB Network’s production beginning at noon with a pre-draft show through the 10th pick. Coverage will move to MLB for Picks 11 to 40. MLB.com will carry the rest of the draft, with Rounds 5-20 starting at 10:30 a.m. Sunday.</p><p>“It’s a production months in the making,” said Ian Theodoridis, MLB Network senior producer. “We have so much talent involved in the show in terms of the ex-players; Dan O’Dowd, our resident GM; our prospect analysts/experts, Jim Callis and Carlos Collazo; and we’re adding Cole Hamels, who is unaffiliated with the network but obviously a hometown flavor in Philadelphia.”</p><p>Not to mention a former Cub, but the Cubs don’t pick until No. 23. This is about the Sox, and the MLB Network production team has been giving them a lot of thought, especially considering their surprising rise to first place in the American League Central.</p><p>“They remind me, honestly, of the ’90 and ’91 Braves,” said Marc Caiafa, MLB Network senior vice president of production. “They’ve got all these pieces, and the fact that they have the first pick and what they’re doing without [rehabbing slugger Munetaka] Murakami, that’s what I keep thinking about because the Braves went worst to first, and the White Sox are right there.”</p><p>“It’s a really unique year for the White Sox and the Rays, picking second,” Theodoridis said, “because we have these two very relevant teams in the top of the draft, where it’s usually two teams that are toward the bottom of the standings. This is a year where you could see someone this year or next year. It’s not like how it used to be where it’s four or five years from now.”</p><p>Speaking of those prospects, MLB Network has more than 200 accounted for with highlight packages and up to 800 with graphics. Each analyst is assigned players to know inside and out to be able to discuss them whenever they’re called.</p><p>One of those analysts is Lance Brozdowski of the Cubs’ Marquee Sports Network. He has made a name for himself in the analytics world and makes occasional appearances on MLB Network, including during the draft combine last month.</p><p>“I don’t know if there’s three of four other people in the country that could do what he does,” Theodoridis said. “His skill isn’t just that he knows data, it’s explaining the data. He makes it very digestible. He’s really comfortable on camera, knows everyone, does great prep work. He’s who we lean on because all of this stuff has become so geared toward analytics.”</p><p>MLB Network has more than draft coverage to produce in Philadelphia. It essentially will serve as a production house for NBC’s All-Star Futures Game on Sunday, Netflix’s Home Run Derby on Monday and the All-Star Game world feed Tuesday, in addition to digital programming.</p><p>“Some of the events may have a different logo before them, but I can assure you that our hands are on everything,” Caiafa said. “But that just speaks to the relationship we have with Fox [which airs the All-Star Game], NBC, Netflix and the league.”</p><p>But Sox fans’ focus will be on the draft, and by the sound of it, they can’t lose whichever player the team picks.</p><p>“I think they’re going to get a generational player either way,” said MLB Network coordinating producer Chris Roenbeck, who with Theodoridis are in their fourth year leading the network’s draft coverage. “They’re going to get probably one of the best college shortstops to come out since probably Dansby Swanson [in 2015]. Or they’re going to get probably the best hitting prep shortstop that we’ve seen in a long time.</p><p>“Our job coming on is to build that drama — who will we see No. 1? That’s what you’re going to see for the first 40 minutes of our coverage before the first pick is announced.”</p><h3>Remote patrol</h3><h3></h3><p>Chicago Sports Network will carry the national broadcasts of the Bulls’ Summer League games. The game Friday against the Grizzlies will air at 10 p.m. on tape delay. The others – Monday against the Jazz at 8, Tuesday against the Wizards at 7 and Thursday against the Lakers at 5 — will air live.</p><p>• The NHL will reveal opening-night matchups for next season Wednesday on ESPN before the ESPY Awards begin at 7 p.m. The full schedule will be released at noon Thursday, with 84 games per team, including two additional division games.</p><p>• ESPN picked up the Cubs’ home game against the Tigers on July 22. >Lung transplants extend lives of sickest cancer patients better than standard treatment, study finds</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wkuudjd-l-h/" target="_blank" >Kaitlin Washburn</a></h5><p><b>Landmark study</b>: A new landmark study from Northwestern Medicine found that patients with advanced lung cancer are far more likely to survive if they receive a lung transplant compared to patients who undergo standard cancer treatment.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the U.S. The medical community has long considered it too risky to transplant lungs into patients with advanced cancer because of the potential risk for cancer cells to spread to the new lungs. But the study published Wednesday challenges that notion, said study co-author Dr. Ankit Bharat, of Northwestern.</p><p><b>Zooming in</b>: Jodi Graf, 61, is one of many patients who participated in Northwestern's study, after her doctors in Houston found a cancerous mass on her lungs in 2023. Graf was too sick to undergo chemotherapy or surgery to remove it. entries.title: Lanes reopened after crash along DuSable Lake Shore Drive on Near South Side
entries.summary: <p>Traffic is moving again near a traffic crash that earlier caused lane closures on DuSable Lake Shore Drive Thursday morning on the Near South Side. </p><p>At 8 a.m., lanes were reopened after the collision, which happened in the northbound lanes in the 2200 block of South DuSable Lake Shore Drive, according to an alert from the Office of Emergency Management and Communications.</p><p>Chicago police responded to a call of service in the area but couldn’t immediately provide details. </p>

entries.title: West Pullman shooting leaves 2 critically hurt
entries.summary: <p>Two 35-year-old men were listed in critical condition at a hospital after assailants opened fire as they were inside an SUV in West Pullman early Thursday. </p><p>The shooting happened about 12:20 a.m. in the 11600 block of South Ada Street, leaving the men, both of whom suffered multiple gunshot wounds to their bodies, in critical condition at Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn, police isad. </p><p>No other injuries were reported and no arrests have been made. </p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Pedestrian seriously injured in hit-and-run on DuSable Lake Shore Drive near Maggie Daley Park
entries.summary: <p>A man was seriously injured in a hit-and-run Wednesday night near Maggie Daley Park.</p><p>The man was walking east in the 100 block of South DuSable Lake Shore Drive when a black vehicle ran a red light, struck him and fled the scene, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in serious condition, police said. </p><p>Area 3 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Elderly father is keen to hit the open road
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> At 82, my father continues to live alone and unassisted. He's generally in good health but is starting to recognize that he won't be forever. One thing he really wants to do while he still can (or thinks he can) is take a road trip — by himself — to visit his sister on the other side of the country.</p><p>He regularly does shorter drives (two to three hours) and figures if he takes his time, he can make the 2,000-mile journey by doing many short stretches over a few days. I think it is a colossally bad idea. He is underestimating the fatigue he's going to experience after a long day of driving and is forgetting how much extra energy it takes to navigate in an unfamiliar place. I'm worried he's going to get in an accident or get lost.</p><p>After telling him all that, and that he's got better options, I offered to pay for a plane ticket. But he doesn't like the idea of trying to navigate an airport (which makes no sense to me compared to driving), or trying to drive an unfamiliar rental car when he arrives. I've suggested going with him, but he wants to stay for a long visit, and there isn't room for me at my aunt's.</p><p>Dad has got his mind set on this trip, and I'm worried he's going to leave without telling anyone he's going. If I can't reason with him, what can I do? We don't live close to each other, and I don't have any right to take his keys, but this is nuts, right? — <i>SEES A DISASTER IN OHIO</i></p><p><b>DEAR SEES:</b> Whether you or I think your father's plan is nuts is beside the point. He is going to make the trip. However, this does not mean you cannot have some input and assurances.</p><p>Help your father plan and map out his trip. Note what hotels or motels there are along the way and help him make reservations. Then get his promise to call you every evening when he checks in so you can know he is all right. It may take some work on your part, but the reassurance of being able to track his progress would be priceless.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My youngest child (early teens) has a hard time making and keeping friends, but he made a new friend three weeks ago. I have met the mom once, briefly, and mostly texted to discuss timing for plans with my kid and hers.</p><p>The mom keeps asking me for money. Our stories are similar, and I've filled her in — divorced, single mom, no contact with ex, no support. Most recently, she texted me asking for gas money and additional money to help fund a trip out of state for a funeral. I may live in a nice house, but I have no help in paying for it plus all the other life expenses. I've told her as much, but I still get these requests.</p><p>I don't want to be rude to her, but I feel like my next step is to be blunt. However, I don't want to risk hurting the friendship between the kids. How do I make it clear without doing damage? — <i>DOLLARS AND SENSE</i></p><p><b>DEAR D & S:</b> Resist the urge to be blunt. Simply tell the woman nicely that you don't have funds to give her at this time. When she asks again, repeat as necessary.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>For an excellent guide to becoming a better conversationalist and a more sociable person, order "How to Be Popular." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Popularity Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Supreme Court finally addressing constitutional constraints on gun ownership
entries.summary: <p>Over the course of 12 days last month, the Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/06/18/supreme-court-makes-it-clear-there-is-no-drug-exception-to-the-second-amendment/" target="_blank" >upheld</a> the gun rights of cannabis consumers, <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/06/25/scotus-overturns-hawaiis-default-rule-against-guns-on-private-property-open-to-the-public/" target="_blank" >rejected</a> Hawaii's default rule against firearms on private property open to the public and <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/01/the-supreme-court-agrees-to-address-the-constitutionality-of-assault-weapon-bans/" target="_blank" >agreed</a> to address the constitutionality of "assault weapon" bans. That flurry of Second Amendment activity underlines the point that supposedly sensible gun regulations are not necessarily consistent with the right to arms as it was historically understood.</p><p>When Congress enacted the <a class="Link" href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-82/pdf/STATUTE-82-Pg1213-2.pdf" target="_blank" >Gun Control Act</a> in 1968, legislators took it for granted that an "unlawful user" of marijuana, depressants, stimulants or narcotics should not be allowed to own a gun. They <a class="Link" href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-100/pdf/STATUTE-100-Pg449.pdf" target="_blank" >reaffirmed</a> that judgment in 1986, changing the wording to encompass unlawful users of "any controlled substance."</p><p>Although the latter law was dubbed the Firearms Owners' Protection Act, it obviously did not protect gun owners with a taste for politically disfavored intoxicants, or even gun owners who dared to use medications prescribed for friends or relatives. It treated all those people as <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/07/21/hunter-biden-walks-free-while-this-iowa-man-serves-4-years-for-the-same-crime/" target="_blank" >felons</a>.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0d0000" name="module-0d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>That policy, the Supreme Court unanimously <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1234_g2bh.pdf" target="_blank" >ruled</a> on June 18, is unconstitutional unless there is evidence that a particular drug user's gun possession would pose a danger to himself or others. It rejected the Trump administration's attempt to prosecute a Texas cannabis consumer who owned a pistol, saying the government may not strip people of their Second Amendment rights simply because they are marijuana users.</p><p>The justices reached that conclusion based on "this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation"— the <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/20-843_7j80.pdf" target="_blank" >lodestar</a> of the court's Second Amendment jurisprudence. Applying the same test a week later, six justices <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1046_nmio.pdf" target="_blank" >said</a> Hawaii had violated the Second Amendment by making it illegal for carry-permit holders to bring guns into a private business without the owner's explicit permission.</p><p>As Hawaii presented it, that presumptive gun ban merely aimed to protect preexisting property rights. But as Justice Samuel Alito noted in the majority opinion, Hawaii's law "departs sharply from the standard common-law rule on access to private property held open to the public."</p><p>Under that rule, "Everyone, including those lawfully carrying firearms, may enter unless expressly prohibited from doing so," Alito wrote. "By contrast, under the new Hawaii law, no one carrying a firearm may enter without the property owner's express authorization."</p><p>That switch, Alito noted, imposed "severe restrictions on the daily activities" of residents with carry permits. Nor was that effect incidental, since Hawaii was attempting an <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2022/07/13/politicians-defy-the-supreme-courts-ruling-on-the-right-to-bear-arms/" target="_blank" >end run</a> around the Supreme Court's 2022 <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/20-843_7j80.pdf" target="_blank" >decision</a> recognizing a constitutional right to carry handguns in public for self-defense.</p><p>Five days after it overturned Hawaii's law, the court <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/orders/courtorders/063026zor_3f14.pdf" target="_blank" >agreed to hear</a> a pair of cases involving bans on widely owned rifles that politicians tendentiously describe as "assault weapons." A dozen states, beginning with California in 1989, have enacted such laws, which hinge on <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2018/05/14/assault-weapons-explained/" target="_blank" >arbitrarily prohibited features</a> such as folding stocks, pistol grips and barrel shrouds.</p><p>The rifles targeted by these laws are <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/06/25/scotus-overturns-hawaiis-default-rule-against-guns-on-private-property-open-to-the-public/" target="_blank" >rarely used</a> by criminals but commonly used by law-abiding Americans, who own <a class="Link" href="https://www.nssf.org/articles/nssf-releases-most-recent-firearm-production-figures-3/" target="_blank" >more than 30 million</a> of them. The latter point is constitutionally relevant because the Supreme Court has <a class="Link" href="https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep554/usrep554570/usrep554570.pdf" target="_blank" >said</a> the Second Amendment applies to "bearable arms" that are "in common use" for "lawful purposes like self-defense."</p><p>The long-simmering <a class="Link" href="https://assets.nationbuilder.com/firearmspolicycoalition/pages/6277/attachments/original/1756312820/2025.08.27_Cert_Petition.pdf" target="_blank" >question</a> posed by these cases is whether the Second Amendment guarantees "the right to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles." If so, other restrictions on the arms Americans are allowed to buy, such as <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/07/doj-challenges-denvers-assault-weapon-ban-and-colorados-magazine-limit/" target="_blank" >magazine limits</a> and California's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/06/the-doj-challenges-virginias-assault-firearm-law-and-californias-glock-ban/" target="_blank" >handgun specifications</a>, may be vulnerable to constitutional challenges.</p><p>The decided cases also have potentially broad implications. If drug use, by itself, does not justify disarming someone, what about a <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/06/12/17-years-ago-she-lost-her-gun-rights-for-passing-a-bad-check-she-wants-scotus-to-rectify-that-injustice/" target="_blank" >nonviolent felony conviction</a>? And if Hawaii's broad restriction on public gun possession was unconstitutional, the far-reaching, location-specific bans imposed by states such as <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2023/12/01/california-defies-scotus-by-imposing-myriad-new-restrictions-on-public-gun-possession/" target="_blank" >California</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2022/10/07/a-federal-judge-rejects-new-yorks-attempt-to-defy-the-scotus-decision-upholding-the-right-to-bear-arms/'" target="_blank" >New York</a> likewise seem legally dubious.</p><p>Nearly two decades after recognizing a constitutional right to arms, the Supreme Court is beginning to address lingering questions about its contours. Control-happy politicians probably will not like the answers.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-400000" name="module-400000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: McConnell, Platner cut from the same entitled cloth
entries.summary: <p>The two men could not be more different. One, a Republican, octogenarian, seven-term Southern senator, the other a progressive, millennial Maine oysterman who’s never spent a day in elected office.</p><p>But Mitch McConnell, the senior senator from Kentucky who’s been MIA for the past few weeks and Graham Platner, the Maine Senate candidate who finally heeded calls to drop out of his race against Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Wednesday night, apparently do have something in common: an outsized sense of entitlement.</p><p>McConnell, who is 84 and not running for reelection, has been hospitalized for three weeks, and yet we still don’t fully know what he was admitted for or what his condition is. Per <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/07/politics/mitch-mcconnell-hospitalization-health" target="_blank" >CNN</a>, “His office has not disclosed a medical reason for the hospitalization or provided specifics on his health status beyond saying last week that he ‘continues to improve’ and ‘is working closely with his staff on Kentucky and Senate matters.’ ”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a40000" name="module-a40000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>While several legislators have said they’ve talked to him and insist he sounds strong, <a class="Link" href="https://www.thedailybeast.com/maga-senator-admits-truth-about-mitch-mcconnells-condition/" target="_blank" >others have said</a> they are completely in the dark. One MAGA influencer, Laura Loomer, <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/LauraLoomer/status/2074210061447307773" target="_blank" >posted</a> ”High level source close to the White House tells me ‘Mitch McConnell is officially brain dead. He’s not coming back.’ ”</p><p>Meanwhile, up in Maine, Platner was artfully dodging calls from his own party to drop out of his race after several allegations of misconduct from women, including a sexual assault allegation from a former girlfriend, came to light. While Platner, who managed to survive a Nazi-tattoo scandal, a sexting scandal and several old tweets scandals, denies the allegations, he did not quit until this week.</p><p>High-profile Democrats including Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., the latter of whom had unsuccessfully hand-selected Maine Gov. Janet Mills to face Collins instead of Platner, did urge Platner to drop out, while other Dems have accused him of trying to influence the picking of his replacement.</p><p>Maine Democratic Party Executive Director Devon Murphy-Anderson released a <a class="Link" href="https://www.mediaite.com/media/news/maine-dem-leader-blasts-platner-teams-attempt-to-put-their-thumb-on-the-scale-of-race-as-pressure-mounts-to-drop-out/" target="_blank" >statement</a> Tuesday, which said in part:</p><p>“Unfortunately, Graham Platner’s team has repeatedly reached out to us in an attempt to put their thumb on the scale of what this process looks like. We have repeatedly reiterated to Graham Platner’s team that they have no role in determining our next Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate nor in determining what this process looks like.”</p><p>Both incidents show a deep lack of accountability to voters, who in one case deserve to know whether their senator is capable of performing his duties, and in another deserve a candidate who isn’t being accused of crimes, bigotry and deception.</p><p>The offensive and odious entitlement of both McConnell and Platner stands out not because it is particularly unique among today’s political class. Tom Kean, the New Jersey GOP congressman, missed more than 100 votes, only sharing after a three-month mystery absence that he was dealing with depression.</p><p>Former President Joe Biden’s Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin failed to disclose a hospitalization for prostate cancer surgery, flouting the established rules for Cabinet members and senior U.S. officials.</p><p>From Biden’s insistence on running for reelection despite his obvious cognitive and political weaknesses to Donald Trump’s brazen flouting of laws and norms, few politicians seem to appreciate that their public service job comes with responsibilities to constituents, including transparency and honesty.</p><p>Both parties increasingly justify the chicanery, because the stakes of winning elections and keeping power are simply too high. But that’s no excuse. If we’ve learned anything over the past decade, it’s that character and accountability do, in fact, matter. And when we, the voters, stop caring about it, well, so do they.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8a0000" name="module-8a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Ranking the Bears' position groups for 2026
entries.summary: <p>Shield your eyes, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> traditionalists. Ranking the Bears by position group entering training camp produces far more offensive standouts than those who play defense:</p><h3>1. Tight end</h3><p>The Bears have one of the best tight end rooms in the NFL. After using a first-round pick, second-round pick and a third-round pick at the position, they better.</p><p>The Bears were one of only three teams last year to have two tight ends total at least 300 yards, 30 catches and two touchdowns apiece. From Week 9-17, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/21/te-colston-loveland-was-a-surprise-draft-pick-by-bears-last-year-at-no-10-and-now-its-time-for-stardom" target="_blank" >Colston Loveland</a> ranked fifth among all tight ends in catches, receiving yards and touchdowns. He became the only rookie tight end in NFL history to have at least eight catches and 100 yards in a postseason game when the Bears beat the Packers.</p><p>The Bears added Stanford’s Sam Roush in Round 3, which will encourage coach Ben Johnson to keep playing with two- and three-tight end sets. The Bears used two tight ends 33% of the time last year, which ranked sixth, and three tight ends 9% of the time, which ranked fifth.</p><h3>2. Wide receiver</h3><p>The Bears’ decision to trade DJ Moore in the name of salary cap flexibility required tremendous faith in the players he leaves behind — namely, Rome Odunze and Luther Burden. The latter has Bears bosses crackling with excitement, while Odunze needs to find a way to produce on the field and manage a nagging foot injury off of it.</p><p>Almost 40% of Burden’s regular season receiving yards came in the last four games, a surge that gave the Bears confidence he could handle an increased target share this year.</p><p>Odunze said he’s facing a “new normal” after dealing with a stress fracture and catching just 44 balls. The Bears need him to stay healthy — Kalif Raymond is next on the depth chart, followed by unproven pieces looking to fill the Moore-sized hole in the roster.</p><h3>3. Offensive line</h3><p>After patching their pass rush last year, the Bears have to do it again. Pro Bowl center Drew Dalman’s sudden retirement prompted the trade for Garrett Bradbury and drafting of second-rounder Logan Jones. Left tackle Ozzy Trapilo’s patellar tendon injury gives Braxton Jones yet another chance to hang on.</p><p>Otherwise, the Bears have stars in guard Joe Thuney, the winner of the NFL’s first Protector of the Year Award, and Darnell Wright, who will become one of the NFL’s best-paid right tackles if he and the Bears can reach a contract extension before Week 1.</p><h3>4. Quarterback</h3><p>Caleb Williams isn’t the top player in the NFL, despite what Packers star Micah Parsons once intimated. Nor is he bad at his job, despite what Fox analyst Mark Schlereth thinks.</p><p>The reality is somewhere in the vast distance in between. This is the season we find out exactly where that is — just in time for the Bears to decide just how much to offer Williams in a contract extension.</p><p>Williams was a wizard late in games last year. The Bears need him to be more efficient long before it gets to that point. His completion percentage above expectation was the worst in football among all quarterbacks not named Brady Cook last year. His 58.1 completion percentage was the 38<sup>th</sup>-best in a league with just 32 starters.</p><p>Remarkably, Williams hasn’t missed a minute due to injury over two years. Tyson Bagent ranks in the top half of NFL backups, though he’s been limited to mostly preseason work.</p><h3>5. Safety</h3><p>Safety will be the greatest test of the Bears’ instincts. General manager Ryan Poles, Johnson and defensive coordinator Dennis Allen let all-pro Kevin Byard leave and chose to give a three-year, $40 million deal to the versatile Coby Bryant.</p><p>Former second-round pick Jaquan Brisker signed with the Steelers. With questions to answer at edge rusher and offensive line, the Bears chose to draft Oregon’s Dillon Thieneman 25<sup>th</sup> overall to replace him. It marked the first time since 1990 the team used a first-round pick at the position.</p><p>The Bears invested in their future, even if Bryant and Thieneman will have to play well to be an immediate upgrade over last year’s duo.</p><h3>6. Running back</h3><p>The Bears were the only team to have two players finish in the top 26 in rushing yards last year — tidy work for D’Andre Swift, who was coming off his worst season, and seventh-round rookie Kyle Monangai. Even more meaningfully, they combined to miss only one game — Swift sat out in Cincinnati when the rookie ran for 176 yards.</p><p>Roschon Johnson and Brittain Brown aren’t particularly compelling backups, but their head coach’s play-calling could make them relevant rushers in a pinch.</p><h3>7. Cornerback</h3><p>The three players slotted to start at cornerback — Jaylon Johnson, Tyrique Stevenson and slot Kyler Gordon — combined to play 31% of the Bears’ defensive snaps last year because of injury and ineffectiveness. Even when he played, Johnson said he wasn’t his normal self. Gordon’s offseason soft-tissue issues make it even easier doubt the Bears’ dependability.</p><p>The team hope the trio can stay healthy enough to play closer to 80% of their snaps, the way they did two years ago. If not, a unit that was once the unquestioned strength of the franchise will continue to be a question mark, particularly after they let Pro Bowl player Nahshon Wright leave for a cheap contract with the Jets.</p><h3>8. Linebacker</h3><h3></h3><p>In their offseason quest to get faster, the Bears cut Tremaine Edmunds and signed Devin Bush to a three-year, $30 million deal. After not living up to his draft status — he was picked 10<sup>th</sup> by the Steelers in 2019 — Bush posted his best season last year with the Browns, finishing as Pro Football Focus’ fourth-best linebacker.</p><p>He and T.J. Edwards, who is recovering from a broken leg, form a solid tandem, with D’Marco Jackson and Jack Sanborn fighting for the strong-side linebacker job and special teams snaps.</p><h3>9. Special teams</h3><p>The Bears let long snapper Scott Daly walk — he signed with the Buccaneers — and will have Luke Elkin and Beau Gardner battle during training camp. If they struggle, the Bears could always add a vet on the eve of the season.</p><p>Tory Taylor, to whom Elkin snapped at Iowa, ranked 11<sup>th</sup> in punting average last year. Kicker Cairo Santos went 25-for-30, with one miss coming from 58 yards.</p><h3>10. Defensive line</h3><p>The only three NFL teams giving more 2026 salary cap money to edge rushers this year are paying T.J. Watt, Maxx Crosby and Brian Burns, who have 16 combined Pro Bowl nods. The Bears, meanwhile, will have Montez Sweat and Dayo Odeyingbo counting combined $45.6 million against the cap. Odeyingbo had one sack last year before tearing his Achilles’ tendon and needs to make an impact for the unit to resemble a threat. Austin Booker is cheap and coming off a strong second half.</p><p>The Bears didn’t add much on the inside, either, after finishing sixth from the bottom in rushing yards allowed.<br></p>

entries.title: Art is all around you at the Obama Presidential Center
entries.summary: <p>Barack and Michelle Obama are well-documented art lovers. So it’s little surprise that the new Obama Presidential Center features several contemporary artists in the prime of their careers, from Mark Bradford and Rashid Johnson to Chicagoans Theaster Gates Look up in the atrium and you’ll see a striking black-and-white photo collage running 175 feet atop the room: “<b>To See What They Could See”</b> is the work of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2025/09/19/theaster-gates-art-smart-museum-university-of-chicago-unto-thee-rebuild" target="_blank" ><b><u>Theaster Gates</u></b><u>,</u></a> a West Side native whose work is now the subject of major exhibitions in New York and Japan. (His first Chicago solo show was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2025/09/19/theaster-gates-art-smart-museum-university-of-chicago-unto-thee-rebuild" target="_blank" ><u>just last year.)</u></a> Gates reprinted photography from the Johnson Publishing Co. archives onto aluminum friezes, creating a historic mural of everyday Black residents — homemakers, students, activists — participating in rallies, marches and peaceful gatherings.</p><p>Walk downstairs in the Forum, near the cafe and store, and you’re positioned to see one of the largest scale works in the center. <b>Mark Bradford’s “City of Big Shoulders”</b> stretches three floors with its artist interpretation of the South Side colored in pinks, yellows and reds. The vibrant blue of the lake angles dramatically across the canvas and is easily viewed without a museum ticket.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Chicago-born director Alex Russell and jazz musician Rob Mazurek to appear at Mubi Fest
entries.summary: <p>Mubi Fest returns to Chicago with a creatively curated lineup of indies and art house fare. From sneak peeks at two of the London-based company’s summer releases to anniversary screenings of four classics, the weekendlong event is also a chance to catch up on three Mubi hits from the Chicago International Film Festival last fall.</p><p>This is the third year that the global film streamer, distributor and producer selected Chicago as its sole North American site for the event. The international fest started in São Paulo, Brazil, in 2022. Since then, Mubi has programmed and presented its short fests in 10 countries.</p><p>The theme of this year’s festival is “Better Together,” which yields “a variety of cinematic pairings that reflect and refract one another, each film either echoing or complicating the other,” Lilly Riber, Mubi’s chief marketing officer, said in an email.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-df0000" name="module-df0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>MUBI Fest Chicago</h3><br>When: July 10-12<br>Where: Music Box Theatre, 3733 N. Southport Ave.; Gene Siskel Film Center, 164 N. State St.; The Salt Shed, 1357 N. Elston Ave.<br>Tickets: $13, $15.50 and $21.38<br>Info: <a class="Link" href="http://mubifest.com/chicago" target="_blank" ><u>mubifest.com/chicago</u></a><br></div> </div><p>The pairings of new titles include repertory screenings:<b> </b>a 10th anniversary sing-along showing of “Popstar: Never Stop Never Stopping”; the 25th anniversary of “Ocean’s Eleven”; the 25th anniversary of “The Royal Tenenbaums”; the 40th anniversary of “The Fly”; and “Sleepaway Camp,” a teen slasher cult hit from 1983. Each title is thematically paired with another film, respectively: “Lurker,” “The Mastermind,” "Rosebush Pruning," “The Substance” and “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.” (Note: Not all of the paired titles are booked as double features in the same theater in back-to-back time slots.)</p><p>Two high-profile movies will be making Chicago premieres. Buzzy horror film “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” set for a national theatrical release Aug. 7, quickly sold out. Filmmaker Jane Schoenbrun continues their metamedia focus in 2024’s “I Saw the TV Glow.” This time a young filmmaker (Hannah Einbinder), schooled in horror theory, it seems, meets an aged “Final Girl” (Gillian Anderson) from an old slasher franchise.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" </div><p></p><h3>“The Mastermind” </h3><p>Josh O’Connor plays a Massachusetts family man who stages a daylight theft of four Arthur Dove paintings in 1970 in this 2025 film that had its Chicago premiere last fall at the Chicago International Film Festival. “Art School Dropout Robs Museum” reads a headline. This hapless son of a county judge hits the road, ending up in an Ohio police wagon for the wrong reason. Two of his priceless lines from different encounters in this deftly understated story: “You don’t look like cops” and “Are you guys cops?” Self-described “abstractivist” Rob Mazurek, a longtime contributor to Chicago’s jazz scene, comes back and plays with the Mastermind Quartet for a live performance of his score commissioned by writer/director Kelly Reichardt. Miles Davis’ trumpet score for a 1958 French film about criminals on the run was “a kind of benchmark” for his own score, Mazurek said in an email. He remembers watching that Louis Malle film titled “Elevator to the Gallows” at the Music Box. “I fantasized long ago about performing in this theater.” (3:30 p.m. Sunday, Music
