entries.title: Relatives remember third child killed in Lake Geneva boating accident as 'bright light'
entries.summary: <p>The third child killed in a Lake Geneva boating crash has been identified by family members as they hope to raise money for children’s charities in her honor.</p><p>Kathryn Schmidt, 10, was identified in a <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/honoring-kate-schmidts-legacy" target="_blank" >fundraiser</a> set up by her family that aims to donate funds to children who can't afford to play the sports she enjoyed like tennis and softball and for those who wish to adopt an animal. </p><p>As of late Thursday morning, the fundraiser has garnered nearly $37,000.</p><p>"This is something that will keep her memory shining in our lives and in the lives of others, carrying forward the love and generosity she always showed," Kathryn's family said in a post attached to the fundraiser. </p><p>Kathryn — who many knew as "Kate" — "didn't have a mean bone in her body," according to the post. </p><p>"Her kindness and joy touched everyone she met, and our family will miss her deeply," relatives wrote. </p><p>Kathryn is the cousin of siblings 6-year-old Caleb Oswald and 7-year-old Abigail Oswald, who also died in the accident, according to the post. </p><p>A spokesperson for the Batavia Public School District 101, where Kate attended school, offered condolences in a statement Thursday. </p><p>"Our hearts are with all of the families affected by this unimaginable tragedy," the school district's statement said.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/08/family-of-2-siblings-killed-in-lake-geneva-boat-accident-raise-money-to-support-charity-in-their-memory" target="_blank" >similar fundraiser</a> was launched by their family to raise funds for children's charities in their memory. Over $220,000 has been raised for that fundraiser. </p><p>The three children were on a boat in Lake Geneva, Wisconsin last Friday when the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/06/lake-geneva-boat-capsize-wheaton-batavia" target="_blank" >boat capsized</a> as a severe storm system swept across Walworth County with peak winds between 90 and 100 mph.<br></p>
entries.author: Mohammad Samra

entries.title: Curse of PCA? Ex-GM talks Pete Crow-Armstrong trade with Cubs that Mets would obviously like to have back
entries.summary: <p>The Red Sox traded Babe Ruth to the Yankees and were cursed for nearly nine decades.</p><p>The Mets traded Pete Crow-Armstrong to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> and … well, who knows what will happen?</p><p>Or not happen.</p><p>Comparing Crow-Armstrong, the Cubs’ All-Star center fielder, to the Great Bambino has been common of late, after the 24-year-old <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/02/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-player-of-the-month-june-stats-babe-ruth-lou-gehrig-shohei-ohtani" >put up a spectacular June</a> that stood alongside months from Ruth and Lou Gehrig as one of baseball’s all-time statistical best.</p><p>And with the last-place Mets reeling – they fired manager Carlos Mendoza after the Cubs pulled off a dominant four-game sweep last month – maybe it’s time to wonder if a team dealing away a star is about to create a new baseball curse.</p><p>Zack Scott was the Mets’ acting general manager at the trade deadline in 2021, taking over after many years in the Red Sox front office. He acquired 2018 MVP runner-up and two-time All Star shortstop Javier Baez – who helped end another infamous baseball curse in 2016 – to give the Mets a late-summer boost, sending Crow-Armstrong, then a prospect just one year removed from being drafted No. 19 overall, to the Cubs in return.</p><p>That boost never came, the Mets finished the season below .500, and Baez left for the Tigers in free agency the following winter, turning out to be nothing but a rental in Queens.</p><p>“When we did that trade, I heard from some of my friends with the Red Sox, who said, ‘I can’t believe you traded for a rental because you hate rentals,” Scott said in a clip from the “Break It Down Show” he posted to Twitter. “It was often my position in the room in Boston to be really opposed to doing anything big for a rental player because it’s such a lopsided future-value negative.</p><p>“That said, when you look at it at the time, when I dissect it and look back and see where did things go wrong, part of that was my bias coming from Boston. [The Red Sox] did not like PCA in the draft. We didn’t like Matt Allan in the draft, either, and that was actually the player the Cubs wanted. So in hindsight, that would have obviously been the much better deal.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Everyone still brings up the Pete Crow-Armstrong trade. He's a star, and I moved him.<br><br>Easy version: I misjudged him. I did. But the real miss is that we were in a pennant race, and the pull to "do something big" moved me off the discipline I'd usually hold.<br><br>A better scouting… <a href="https://t.co/Mw8fQtXAtd">pic.twitter.com/Mw8fQtXAtd</a></p>— Zack Scott (@ZackScottSports) <a href="https://x.com/ZackScottSports/status/2074909941354160460?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 8, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Allan, a righty pitcher and third-round pick of the Mets in 2019, never pitched above Class A in their system.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong, meanwhile, is an MVP candidate for the Cubs, leading baseball’s position players with 5.8 fWAR.</p><p>“Everyone still brings up the Pete Crow-Armstrong trade,” Scott wrote on Twitter. “He’s a star, and I moved him. Easy version: I misjudged him. I did.</p><p>“But the real miss is that we were in a pennant race and the pull to ‘do something big’ moved me off the discipline I’d usually hold. A better scouting report doesn’t fix that. Building the decision so the urge to act doesn’t set the terms does. I own it.”</p>

entries.title: La empresa matriz de Cash App llega a un acuerdo de $45 millones con Illinois y 44 otros estados
entries.summary: <p>Illinois recibirá $1.1 millones de un acuerdo de $45 millones que involucra a 45 estados con la empresa matriz de la aplicación de transferencias de dinero Cash App, acusada de engañar a los clientes sobre la seguridad de la aplicación.</p><p>Block Inc. enfrentará sanciones civiles por $55 millones y también tendrá que pagar a los clientes en todo el país entre $75 millones y $120 millones de dólares como parte del <a class="Link" href="https://www.consumerfinance.gov/enforcement/actions/block-inc/" target="_blank" >acuerdo</a>, que incluye a la Oficina de Protección Financiera del Consumidor.</p><p>En un comunicado, el Fiscal General de Illinois, Kwame Raoul, dijo que el acuerdo responsabiliza a la empresa y exige que "cambie sus prácticas dañinas".</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-440000" name="module-440000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Block dijo a los usuarios de Cash App que su dinero estaba seguro e implicó falsamente que la aplicación funcionaba como un banco, con las mismas protecciones”, declaró Raoul. “Block era consciente de que el fraude en su plataforma estaba aumentando drásticamente y no advirtió a los usuarios, no fortaleció las protecciones ni proporcionó ayuda real a los usuarios cuando las cosas salieron mal”.</p><p>Un portavoz de la empresa confirmó el acuerdo y dijo que la compañía ha realizado "inversiones significativas en protección al consumidor, servicio al cliente y cumplimiento".</p><p>"Compartimos el compromiso de los fiscales generales para abordar los desafíos de la industria y continuamos invirtiendo en operaciones y tecnología para promover un ecosistema financiero seguro y saludable", dijo el portavoz en un comunicado proporcionado al Sun-Times el miércoles por la noche.</p><p>La demanda acusó a la empresa de no prevenir el fraude e incluso de tener sistemas que facilitaban la comisión de dicho fraude. La verificación mínima de identidad permitía a alguien crear cuentas falsas o múltiples, y la empresa no contaba con una línea de asistencia telefónica. En cambio, a los clientes que habían sido defraudados a menudo se les proporcionaban números de teléfono de asistencia al cliente falsos por esos estafadores, alegó la demanda.</p><p>Como parte del acuerdo, la empresa debe ofrecer al menos 13.5 horas de líneas telefónicas atendidas por humanos por día como parte del apoyo de 24 horas, así como reembolsar a los clientes por transacciones fraudulentas, dejar de comercializar la aplicación como segura y educar a los usuarios sobre los peligros del fraude.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: White Sox put reliever Trevor Richards on family emergency list, recall Tyler Davis
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox made a roster move Thursday, but it's not the one fans are awaiting. </p><p>The team put right-hander Trevor Richards on the Bereavement/Family Medical Emergency List and recalled right-hander Tyler Davis from Triple-A Charlotte. Slugger Munetaka Murakami is close to returning from a strained right hamstring, and his impending arrival will necessitate a roster move.</p><p>Richards, 33, has been pitching well of late, including two high-leverage situations last week in Cleveland in which he combined for 3 1/3 scoreless innings with five strikeouts. In his last 18 outings, he has a 1.37 ERA (four earned runs in 26 1/3 innings).</p><p>Since being acquired by the Sox on May 5 for cash considerations, Richards has a 3.48 ERA (12 earned runs in 31 innings) with 30 strikeouts in 22 relief appearances </p><p>Davis, 27, has made four relief appearances for Charlotte (three earned runs in 4 2/3 innings) since being optioned June 21. He had a 4.63 ERA (12 earned runs in 23 1/3 innings) with 20 strikeouts in 22 relief outings from April 23 to June 20 in his first major-league stint.<br></p>

entries.title: 'The kids feel it' — summer camp has kids singing the blues
entries.summary: <p>What is the blues? The blues is pain set to music.</p><p>Take "I'd Rather Go Blind," the 1967 classic written by blues queen Etta James. Beaten by her drunken foster father, James spent time in Cook County Jail for forging checks to support her longtime heroin habit. You can hear it in her voice.</p><p>Posing definite artistic challenges for singers who are not Etta James, such as a high school student from the Northwest suburbs.</p><p>"Something toooooold me, it was oh-oh-ver," sings Nyrobi, 17, slowly, in a thin, wavering voice, on a small stage on the first floor of Columbia College, 1014 S. Michigan on Wednesday. "When I saw youuuuu with her, talking. Something deep down in my sooooul...."</p><p>Jackie Scott interrupts.</p><p>"The woman is writing this song because she saw her man with another women," says Scott, an imposing woman with a gold ring on her left hand that spells, "BLUES." "Imagine you saw your boyfriend with another girl. You're not going to be singing."</p><p>And here she delivers a spot-on imitation of Nyrobi's airy warble.</p><p>"You're not going to do that, right?" Scott continues. "You're going to push it out a little more."</p><p>"SOMETHING TOLLLLLLD ME," she belts, in a strong, loud voice. "IT WAS OHHHHHVER!"</p><p>Welcome to day three of Blues Camp Chicago, where the world of summertime childhood fun meets the snap-brim hat and two-tone shoes discipline of blues musicianship. There are studio rehearsals, sound checks and sing-alongs, plus snacks, skating and "sneakerball." </p><p>"We want them to be kids, of course. We want them to understand and appreciate blues, as American roots music," said Fernando Jones, the veteran Chicago blues man who founded Blues Camp Chicago 17 years ago.</p><div class="Enhancement" aria-label="Next"> <svg class="FlickityCustomNavigation-button-icon"><use xlink:href="#icon-right"></use></svg> </button> </div> </div></div> </bsp-carousel> </div> </div><p>About 80 campers, age 5 through 17, from all over the country, take part in the five-day program. They perform several concerts — at Navy Pier, at Reggie's blues club on South State — and are guided by 15 instructors and staff. Some kids arrive barely able to carry a tune; others are aspiring professionals — one brought along a pricey PRS guitar signed by Buddy Guy.</p><p>What is the blues? Not always sad. Muddy Waters "boasting and braying, preening like a peacock" in "Hoochie Coochie Man." The question has been debated in Chicago for at least a century, since a 1917 copyright infringement trial where Judge George A. Carpenter famously quizzed Dominic LaRocca, “The Jazz Kid,” in federal court.</p><p>"May I ask," the judge said, "what are the blues?"</p><p>"The blues is jazz," LaRocca answered. "Jazz is the blues."</p><p>Poet Langston Hughes dissected the blues again and again.</p><p>"When the shoe strings break/On <i>both</i> your shoes," Hughes write. "And you're in a hurry—That's the blues."</p><p>I put the question to the blues kids.</p><p>"I personally think that the blues is just a mix of your emotions," said Tristan, 10. "You put that into an instrument, a synthesizer or even a simple piano. Just your emotions flowing together to make beautiful music."</p><p>The camp is free, funded by Jones's Blues Kids Foundation, and Jones says that while applicants are required to create a video, there isn't a culling process — Blues Camp Chicago accepts everyone who applies, across a range of age, talent and ability. Many have been coming for years.</p><p>Ricky, 10, who plays guitar, is here for his third year. What prompts an 8-year-old to go to blues camp?</p><p>"He heard about the camp and registered, and I can say he's become a little blues head now," said his mother, Nina Garcia-Carpintero, who has seen how the camp has affected him.</p><p>"An amazing camp where kids just create a bond with each other. Very sociable. He meets new friends all the time, keeps in touch with everyone. Beautiful friendships," she said. "And musically, somehow, they all come together. He becomes very confident, feels very expressive as well. He genuinely feels the music. The kids feel it."</p><p>How can a boy entering the fifth grade sing the blues?</p><p>"It's funny, because one of the members from his band always says that, when he plays, it's like he's been through 10 marriages, five divorces and a bunch of kids," said Garcia-Carpintero. "Mr. Jones has done such a great job with these kids. I can't say enough."</p><p>Jones stresses, not just music, but manners, discipline and confidence.</p><p>"I was really shy," said Nyrobi, in her eighth year. "It was really encouraging, opening you up."</p><p>Did she mind being pushed to find her inner Etta James?</p><p>"It's mentoring," said Nyrobi, who plans to go to law school. "I'm still obviously learning. Seventeen years of life, so there's not much heartbreak that can be drawn from it. It's her life experience, to convey that to me, so I can do it in my voice."</p>

entries.title: Judge finds Chicago’s embattled U.S. attorney violated secrecy order in Tren de Aragua case
entries.summary: <p>A federal magistrate judge found Thursday<b> </b>that the Department of Justice<b> </b>failed to honor her order sealing a criminal complaint charging three alleged Tren de Aragua gang members, but she also concluded there was no nefarious purpose behind the violation and she ordered no sanction.</p><p>U.S. Magistrate Judge Laura McNally made her comments during a highly unusual hearing in which she ordered embattled U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros into one of the largest courtrooms in Chicago's federal courthouse. She insisted he stand at a lectern while she discussed what happened in the case. </p><p>McNally said there was a "clear violation of the sealing order. The order was unambiguous." She said the order wasn't lifted until 3 p.m. July 2.</p><p>However, Boutros discussed the case at a July 1 press conference in Washington, with acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel.</p><p>"Your statement acknowledges that you were aware, when you went up there, that there was a sealing order in place," McNally told Boutros.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/03/judge-orders-u-s-attorney-boutros-into-court-over-potential-violations-of-seal-order" >Judge orders U.S. Attorney Boutros into court over ‘potential violations’ of seal order</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Boutros told the judge he took her comments "very seriously."<b> </b>He said his "intentions were to comply with the order." And he told the judge,<b> </b>"I respect your findings."</p><p>Thursday's hearing took place before a fairly full gallery of onlookers in the chief judge's courtroom on the 25th floor of the Dirksen Federal Courthouse. It also came seven weeks<b> </b>into a credibility crisis<b> </b>for Boutros<b> </b>that began with the May 21 collapse of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>the “Broadview Six” case</u></a> over apparent prosecutor misconduct. </p><p>Damage has continued to spread, even in cases unrelated to the six Operation Midway Blitz protesters.</p><p>McNally previously wrote on the court docket<b> </b>that prosecutors called her chambers at 10:05 a.m.<b> </b>the day of the press conference, seeking an order unsealing the criminal complaint, with certain redactions, and claiming they “needed to obtain a ruling within the next 15 minutes.”</p><p>Boutros <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/08/us-attorney-boutros-tren-de-aragua-charges-judge-seal-hearing-court-patel-blanche" target="_blank" >insisted in a court filing</a> Wednesday<b> </b>that he acted in good faith<b> </b>and believed the press conference “complied with the letter and spirit of the sealing order”<b> </b>because it was for the purpose of “facilitating ‘the enforcement of criminal law.'”</p><p>The seal order did “not prohibit law enforcement personnel from disclosing”<b> </b>documents in the case “as necessary to facilitate the enforcement of criminal law,”<b> </b>he pointed out.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/08/us-attorney-boutros-tren-de-aragua-charges-judge-seal-hearing-court-patel-blanche" >U.S. Attorney Boutros still due in court Thursday after failing to convince judge to cancel hearing</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>One purpose of the press conference was to “deter future crimes”<b> </b>by Tren de Aragua “by publicly demonstrating that federal law enforcement would prioritize the prosecution and punishment of violent offenses” they committed, Boutros argued.</p><p>“The U.S. Attorney reasonably believed that disclosure of the arrests and charges of [Tren de Aragua] members helped facilitate the government’s enforcement of criminal law both in and outside of this district,” he wrote.</p><p>McNally rejected that argument Thursday.</p><p>"I would not have signed an order that permitted the full discretion of the entire law enforcement community to decide that, at this point, we think what we're doing here should not be sealed," McNally said. "I would not have granted that motion."</p><p>Boutros dodged at least two other high-stakes hearings in recent weeks. U.S. District Judge Sharon Johnson Coleman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" ><u>threatened to hold a hearing</u></a> in June over allegations of prosecutor misconduct that surfaced in a case over which she presides. Boutros avoided it by permanently dropping charges against two defendants.</p><p>His office also recently convinced U.S. Magistrate Judge Keri Holleb Hotaling<b> </b>to hold off on a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/18/boutros-holleb-hotaling-atf-country-club-hills" target="_blank" ><u>sanctions hearing aimed at the feds</u></a> after a video raised questions about the accuracy of a sworn affidavit in another case.</p><p>Boutros’ team argued that Holleb Hotaling had no authority to hold the hearing. The judge agreed to a “brief” delay and sought input from defense attorneys.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p>

entries.title: Vegas baby as Bulls' Caleb Wilson wants to impress in Summer League
entries.summary: <p>This isn’t your father’s Summer League.</p><p>It might not even be your older brother’s.</p><p>Ten years ago, the Summer League courtside seats were a few veteran teammates coming to watch the young guys, some family members, and boxer Floyd “Money” Mayweather with his entourage.</p><p>Now, it’s a standing-room only event that feels like New York’s famous Rucker Park in the 1970s. A who’s who of NBA royalty watching, while the best young talent in the game tries to put on a highlight show.</p><p>And if this draft class continues living up to the hype of how talented and deep it was, well, Las Vegas is about to get yet another must-see two-week residency.</p><p>There have already been signs of that in the Summer League California Classic last week.</p><p>Utah’s Darryn Peterson looks like he can be a real problem for opposing teams already, playing in two games on the West Coast and dropping 53 total points with 14 assists. No cramping, no load management, no concerns for the No. 2 overall pick.</p><p>No. 3 pick Cameron Boozer dropped 15 points with four rebounds and four assists in his debut in Salt Lake, giving Memphis that warm feeling they made the right selection last month.</p><p>And the good news that every Bulls fan should be smiling about? Their team’s No. 4 pick in Caleb Wilson wants to beat them all. He said as much in his introductory presser, insisting that he felt like he was the top player in the rookie class and wanted to make sure No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa, Peterson and Boozer all feel that starting in July.</p><p>Good news, Rook, you’ll get that chance.</p><p>The Bulls tip off Summer League Friday night by taking on Boozer’s Grizzlies team, followed by a Monday tilt with Peterson and Utah, and then a night later against Washington and Dybantsa. Yes, it’s only Summer League, but if a player with Wilson’s confidence and swagger wants to make an early statement, then Vegas is the place.</p><p>His head coach Tiago Splitter is actually coaching several of the Summer League games just to set a tone, which is not the norm, and Wilson will have fellow first-rounder Dailyn Swain (No. 15 overall) and 2025 first rounder Noa Essengue (No. 12 overall) at his side.</p><p>Wilson is on the main stage, but don’t discount the attention the organization will focus on Essengue.</p><p>Drafted as a project, it quickly turned into a red-shirt year thanks to an ongoing shoulder issue that required season-ending surgery.</p><p>Maybe a blessing in disguise as the youngster was able to work on strengthening his body and even added a few inches.</p><p>“Very long and expectations are higher because (he’s a) 6-foot-10, 6-foot-11 player, can put the ball on the floor, shoot a little bit, can do a lot of things,” Splitter said of Essengue. “I want to see him in the games and how he approaches every possession, how he fights every possession. I’m going to put a lot of pressure on Caleb (Wilson), Dailyn (Swain), on Noa. Those are the guys that really push this team in the Summer League and (it will) be contagious with teammates, the effort, how we are going to play, share the ball.</p><p>“We are going to rebound. We’re going to defend. Caleb, Dailyn and Noa, they have to set the tone. I think he (Essengue) can be three, four, five easily.”</p><p>Baby steps. Just let Essengue be healthy and show some flashes. They don’t need him to be a star.</p><p>There'll be plenty of those on display the next few weeks. Just ask Wilson.<br></p>

entries.title: Taste of Chicago 2026 destaca los sabores culinarios internacionales de la ciudad
entries.summary: <p>El festival Taste of Chicago comenzó el miércoles por la mañana con más de 80 vendedores de toda la ciudad, desde puestos de restaurantes locales hasta camiones de comida y pop-ups destacados.</p><p>Y aunque hay muchos clásicos de Chicago disponibles, como Connie’s Pizza, Eli’s Cheesecake y Harold’s Chicken, el festival de este año también muestra los sabores internacionales de la ciudad. Chicago es el hogar de millones de inmigrantes y la selección de este año en Taste lo demuestra, desde la cocina senegalesa hasta las empanadas de estilo argentino.</p><p>Casi el 38% de los restaurantes participantes están estableciendo un puesto en el festival por primera vez, según el Departamento de Asuntos Culturales y Eventos Especiales (DCASE).</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8b0000" name="module-8b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Si ha pasado un tiempo desde tu última visita al Taste of Chicago, encontrarás que el sistema de boletos icónico ha desaparecido para siempre. Todo el evento, al que se puede ingresar gratuitamente, no acepta pagos en efectivo. entries.title: Seiya Suzuki breaks free of mini slump, showing well-stocked Cubs lineup primed to chase championship goals
entries.summary: <p>BALTIMORE – After leaving Thursday’s game late with cramping in his calf, Seiya Suzuki had big plans.</p><p>“I’m going to go eat about 100 bananas,” the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> right fielder said through an interpreter.</p><p>Surely, the Cubs – who aren’t worried about the cramping, by the way – hope the power of potassium keeps Suzuki in the same zone he found himself in the last couple days in Maryland, where he broke free of a mini slump that saw him go hitless in four straight games.</p><p>He smacked a three-run homer in Wednesday’s win and just about delivered another victory single-handedly Thursday, driving in both Cubs runs with a solo homer and an RBI double before the bullpen coughed up the lead in the eighth inning of a 3-2 loss.</p><p>“The last series in Chicago, at home, I couldn’t hit. I had a lot of frustration built up,” Suzuki said. “So really, I was taking that frustration out on the ball.”</p><p>But it’s not just Suzuki striking fear into the hearts of baseballs.</p><p>The Cubs have shown off plenty of impressive batwork of late, highlighted, of course, by that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/01/cubs-dansby-swanson-home-runs-rbis-padres-offense-lineup-craig-counsell-nico-hoerner-pete-crow-armstrong-michael-conforto" >monster offensive series against the Padres</a> on the most recent home stand.</p><p>Taking their show on the road to Baltimore this week, things weren’t quite as thunderous, but it was still apparent – with 16 runs and six homers in a three-game series win – that these Cubs are built to do damage to opposing pitchers in a way that could see them achieve their championship-level goals.</p><p>“It’s a reassuring lineup,” Suzuki said. “The guys in front of me get on base. The guys behind me, they’re great hitters. If I’m on base, they’ll drive me in.</p><p>“Simply put, you look at 1 through 9 in the lineup, there are very good hitters.”</p><p>For a portion of the season, it looked as if center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong might have needed to shoulder the offensive load by himself, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/09/cubs-offense-record-slump-alex-bregman-pete-crow-armstrong-national-league-player-of-the-week" >something he acknowledged wasn’t possible</a> in a team sport, no matter how ridiculous his numbers were.</p><p>Those numbers, by the way, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/08/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-20-20-season-home-runs-stolen-bases-orioles-justin-steele-craig-counsell-hunter-harvey-phil-maton" >are still ridiculous</a>. He walked, doubled and scored Thursday, improving his season OPS to .930.</p><p>“I feel like every time he’s at the plate, he’s getting on first base or hitting a home run or <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/15/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-hit-for-cycle-walk-off-win-rockies-pedro-ramirez-matt-shaw-shota-imanaga" >hitting for the cycle</a>,” first baseman Michael Busch said Thursday. “Honestly, it’s pretty crazy.</p><p>“This game is very difficult, especially in the box. To be able to do that at a high clip is pretty amazing, while also playing some of the best defense in the world. It’s pretty impressive.”</p><p>But a “one-man wrecking crew,” as Crow-Armstrong put it, doesn’t equal a championship-caliber lineup.</p><p>This Cubs one, though? When there are multiple guys clicking simultaneously? It sure looks like it is, well past the extended outage from early in the summer.</p><p>“The key to our offense is it doesn’t have to be the same guy [every game],” manager Craig Counsell said after the game. “We have guys that can do it, kind of carry the load on certain days, and that’s a good sign.”</p><p>Even though Thursday’s two-run output wasn’t enough, the Cubs lineup you’re seeing now, that’s what’s expected from this group. Throughout that stretch, Cubs hitters expressed confidence the worm would turn. That’s what happened.</p><p>Coming into Thursday, the Cubs had the highest on-base percentage in baseball since June 11, at .355. They ranked second in baseball during that span with 161 runs scored and third with 41 home runs. Their team wRC-plus of 130 was the sport’s best.</p><p>This team can get on base. This team can keep the line moving. This team can hit the ball out of the ballpark.</p><p>Not a bad way to chase a trophy.</p><p>“We’ve been able to prove that and show it over the years,” Busch said. “Hitting comes in waves, at times. The better the players you have in the box, those waves are a little smaller. We had a little bit of a tough stretch in May and June.</p><p>“Just watching some of the guys compete, top to bottom, guys coming off the bench, we have a bunch of really good hitters.”</p>

entries.title: Former Chicago-area Mormon figure pleads guilty to child sex crime, could face life in prison
entries.summary: <p>A former Chicago area Mormon church figure who was excommunicated in the 1990s over allegations of child sexual abuse — and quickly reinstated by the faith group, and allowed to serve as a member and leader in an Ohio congregation — pleaded guilty Thursday in a criminal case that accused him of molesting two other children more recently.</p><p>Wade Christofferson, 73, pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in Columbus, Ohio, to coercion and enticement of a minor, which carries a sentence of at least 10 years in prison, and up to a life term.</p><p>He’s expected to be sentenced by Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr. at a later date. If Christofferson ever gets out of custody he will have to register as a sex offender, per the plea agreement.</p><p>An attorney for Christofferson couldn’t immediately be reached for comment.</p><p>Arrested in November, Christofferson was accused in court records of molesting an Ohio child 15 to 20 times.</p><p>He “also allegedly engaged in a sexually explicit FaceTime call with a second minor victim and sent coded letters to her Utah home that referenced sexual activity,” federal prosecutors alleged. “Christofferson also committed hands-on sexual abuse of that child as well.”</p><p>Some if not all of the misconduct occurred in 2025, records show.</p><p>The victims were 10 or under.</p><p>Beyond the horror of the accusations, the case spurred questions about how seriously the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints — the formal name for the Mormon institution — handles child sex abuse allegations and whether offenders are sometimes shown deference over accusers.</p><p>Christofferson’s brother, D. Todd Christofferson, is a top Mormon leader in Utah where the faith system is based. He acknowledged this year through a church spokesman that he learned in or about 2020 that his brother may have molested children many years earlier and didn’t notify police or child welfare authorities.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-590000" name="image-590000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d9276ad/2147483647/strip/true/crop/630x354+0+202/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2F53%2F472894154fb4b1fcaaf5e888671a%2Fscreenshot-2026-03-01-at-10-14-09-pm.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/96e1d63/2147483647/strip/true/crop/630x354+0+202/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2F53%2F472894154fb4b1fcaaf5e888671a%2Fscreenshot-2026-03-01-at-10-14-09-pm.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d6fd319/2147483647/strip/true/crop/630x354+0+202/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F98%2F53%2F472894154fb4b1fcaaf5e888671a%2Fscreenshot-2026-03-01-at-10-14-09-pm.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Mormon church leader D. Todd Christofferson “respected the adult victims’ wishes not to involve law enforcement at that time,” the spokesman has said.</p><p>Wade Christofferson’s more-recent abuse involving other victims didn’t occur on church grounds and wasn’t directly related to church activities, according to records and interviews. However, court records show his cell phone was examined around the time of his arrest and the online history included the search: “in Ohio do clergy have to report child abuse confessions”?</p><p>Court records say he also texted the father of one of his victims in November, saying: “I am deeply sorry for what I have done and will be meeting with my bishop to start the repentance process.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/29/church-of-jesus-christ-of-latter-day-saints-mormon-stories-john-dehlin-d-todd-christofferson-dallin-oaks" target="_blank" >Podcaster in legal battle with Latter-day Saints says church has no legitimate claim over the word ‘Mormon’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>While the Latter-day Saints has, much like the Catholic church, adopted child safety protocols to prevent abuse and deal with a sexual abuse crisis within the ranks, transparency is seen as a key part of prevention and accountability, according to experts.</p><p>If there’s an abuse allegation made against a Catholic priest in Chicago, the cleric is immediately pulled from public ministry and the parish and public are informed about the accusation while investigations are conducted. Once they’re concluded, the public is also informed of the outcome.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Illinois' assault weapons ban upheld by appeals court as U.S. Supreme Court mulls Cook County's prohibition
entries.summary: <p>One week after the U.S. Supreme Court announced it would consider whether there is a Constitutional right<b> </b>to possess assault weapons — by taking up a challenge to Cook County's assault weapons ban — the federal appeals court in Chicago sided Thursday with Gov. JB Pritzker<b> </b>on the validity of Illinois' statewide ban.</p><p>The 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that Illinois' ban on AR-15s and 30-round rifle magazines "are consistent with the principles that underpin our nation's tradition of firearm regulation." Judge<b> </b>Amy St. Eve<b> </b>wrote the opinion, which was joined by<b> </b>Judge<b> </b>Frank Easterbrook.</p><p>Chief Judge Michael Brennan<b> </b>dissented.</p><p>The Supreme Court is likely to have the final say on the Constitutional question — and whether Illinois’ ban ultimately survives. The high court is on track to rule around the five-year anniversary of the 2022<b> </b>Highland Park<b> </b>Fourth of July parade shooting. The massacre, which left seven dead, inspired the statewide assault weapons ban.</p><p>The Highland Park gunman used an AR-15-style semiautomatic rifle.</p><p>Illinois' prohibition on assault weapons was a signature achievement of Gov. JB Pritzker. It bans the sale of assault weapons like the AR-15 and caps the purchase of magazines at 10 rounds for long guns and 15 for handguns. Pritzker, who has not ruled out a 2028 presidential run, signed the ban into law in 2023.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/09/22/donald-trumps-assault-weapons-ban-civil-rights-chief-justice-department-appeals-court-illinois" >Trump’s civil rights boss challenged by appeals court weighing Illinois assault weapons ban</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department’s civil rights division, took the unusual step in September of traveling to Chicago to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/09/22/donald-trumps-assault-weapons-ban-civil-rights-chief-justice-department-appeals-court-illinois" target="_blank" >briefly participate in arguments</a> over the weapons ban before the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.</p><p>Though her portion of the 90-minute hearing lasted about five minutes, the move was hailed by gun-rights advocates who oppose the law.</p><p>Dhillon rejected a previous decision by the appeals court to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2023/11/3/23945656/assault-weapons-ban-upheld" target="_blank" >uphold the assault weapons ban</a>, arguing that the AR-15 and similar guns are “clearly” protected by the Second Amendment.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/20-843_7j80.pdf" target="_blank" >A 2022 U.S. Supreme Court ruling</a> laid out a two-step test for such gun laws. In New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, the justices held that<b> </b>if an individual’s conduct is covered by the Second Amendment, the government must then demonstrate that the law is “consistent with this nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.”</p><p>But the 7th Circuit sided with Pritzker the next year, in 2023, finding that the weapons covered by Illinois’ law don’t have Second Amendment protection because they “are much more like machine guns and military-grade weaponry” than like other firearms used for self-defense.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/07/02/supreme-court-declines-hear-challenge-illinois-assault-weapons-ban" >Battle over Illinois’ assault weapon ban will continue after Supreme Court declines to get involved</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The panel in 2023 was considering whether the law should be blocked by a preliminary injunction. This time around, the judges considered whether to uphold U.S. District Judge Stephen McGlynn’s November 2024 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/11/08/federal-judge-rules-illinois-assault-weapons-ban-unconstitutional" target="_blank" >ruling that the law is unconstitutional</a>.</p><p>The latest panel to rule was made up of three judges appointed by Republican presidents. Easterbrook was appointed by President Ronald Reagan, while Brennan and St. Eve were appointed by President Donald Trump. </p><p>McGlynn, the lower-court judge, was also appointed by Trump. McGlynn opened his 168-page ruling in November 2024 by asking, “why do we protect ourselves with firearms?”</p><p>“Who comes to our aid in times of peril?” he wrote. “Sometimes, it is the police or first responders; other times it is healthcare professionals; and sometimes it is family, friends, or neighbors. Sometimes, it is no one.”</p><p>“The AR-15 is the Rorschach test of America’s gun debate,” he wrote. “In listening to the political debate and in reading various judicial interpretations of what the AR-15 represents, it is obvious that many are seeing very different creatures.”</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/90/d2/c9610c774087adf716e577547041/barnettopinion.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: El crimen en CTA ha disminuido los últimos 6 meses consecutivos, según la jefa de la agencia
entries.summary: <p>El crimen en la Autoridad de Tránsito de Chicago (CTA) ha disminuido durante los últimos seis meses consecutivos en medio de un aumento de la seguridad para abordar un número históricamente alto de ataques violentos.</p><p>La directora interina de la CTA, Nora Leerhsen, presumió de esas cifras durante la reunión de la junta de la agencia el miércoles, señalando una disminución del 30% en todos los delitos reportados en el tránsito durante 2025.</p><p>La caída fue aún más dramática en la Línea Roja, donde la Policía de Chicago y la Oficina del Alguacil del Condado de Cook se han enfocado en aumentar las patrullas desde marzo, tras una amenaza de recorte de fondos por parte de la administración del presidente Donald Trump.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a20000" name="module-a20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La Línea Roja ha visto una disminución del 47% en todos los delitos y una caída del 76% en delitos violentos hasta junio en comparación con el año pasado, dijo Leerhsen.</p><p>"La percepción de seguridad en la CTA se ve afectada por cada incidente que tenemos", dijo Leerhsen. "Pero dada la importancia de nuestro sistema para la vitalidad y fortaleza de nuestra ciudad, es increíblemente importante para mí que aún nos detengamos y notemos este progreso, que es real y se mantiene".</p><p>Leerhsen no mencionó que las agresiones agravadas y los asaltos ahora son menores que en la misma fecha de 2025. Si la tendencia continúa, la CTA podría finalmente haber superado un aumento sostenido de 5 años en los ataques violentos. La CTA cerró 2025 con 469 ataques violentos, el número más alto registrado en los últimos 25 años, informó anteriormente el Sun-Times.</p><p>Leerhsen dijo que la criminalidad ha continuado disminuyendo cada mes desde enero. Nueve de los últimos 11 meses también registraron una disminución en el crimen, dijo.</p><p>Los esfuerzos de combate al crimen en la CTA ahora estarán supervisados por el nuevo jefe de seguridad de la agencia, Joe Bird, quien anteriormente se desempeñó como comandante de la Sección de Transporte Público del Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CPD), según dijo Leerhsen.</p><p>El transporte público de Chicago ha experimentando una gran reestructuración desde la implementación de la Ley de la Autoridad de Transporte del Norte de Illinois (NITA) el 1 de junio.</p><p>La ley salvó a la CTA, Metra y Pace de drásticos recortes de servicio mediante una aportación adicional de $1 mil millones al año. La ley también reemplaza el papel de supervisión de la Autoridad Regional de Transporte (RTA) por una junta de la NITA más poderosa, que debe constituirse antes del 1 de septiembre. La NITA tiene el poder de establecer tarifas y dirigir la planificación entre las agencias de una manera que la RTA no podía.</p><p>La ley despoja notablemente al alcalde Brandon Johnson de algunos poderes, quien ya no tiene la mayoría de los nombramientos en la junta de la CTA. Johnson anunció esta semana sus elecciones para las juntas de la NITA, eligiendo la mayoría de los nombramientos que ya había realizado para la CTA y la RTA. Deben ser aprobados por el Concejo Municipal.</p><h3>Ampliación de cámaras en los carriles de autobús</h3><p>La junta de la CTA aprobó el miércoles una importante expansión de su programa de aplicación automatizada de carriles para autobuses, aumentando el número de cámaras que emiten multas de 6 a 52 autobuses.</p><p>Los autobuses equipados con cámaras han emitido cerca de 22,000 advertencias y multas a vehículos estacionados ilegalmente <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/10/15/automated-ticketing-cameras-added-to-6-downtown-cta-buses" target="_blank" >desde que fueron activados en octubre</a>, dijo Leerhsen. Las cámaras cubren las rutas 20 Madison, 36 Broadway, 66 Chicago y 8 Halsted.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Residents, businesses near Thornton Reservoir endure 'very unpleasant' stench after heavy rainfall
entries.summary: <p>The Thornton Quarry has long been an interesting destination within Chicago’s south suburbs. However, this week the usual sights and smells have been replaced and Thornton Reservoir — sitting at nearly full capacity after weeks of heavy rainfall — continues to emit a foul odor to the area.</p><p>For Alex Ferreira, owner of Blades and Fades barbershop at 100 S. Williams St. in Thornton since 2010, the nearly full reservoir is something he’s never seen before.</p><p>"We've never seen it this full," Ferreira told the Sun-Times as he finished up a trim on a man's hair. "These rains are unheard of around here."</p><p>The Metropolitan Water Reclamation District's Thornton Reservoir, part of the region's Deep Tunnel flood-control system, reached 94% capacity this week after more than 8 inches of rain fell across the Chicago area over the past month. Officials said it marks the fullest the reservoir has been since opening in 2015.</p><p>Ferreira, 37, pointed out that the foul scent is not new. Clients often comment it when they visit the barbershop, he said, comparing it to "roadkill." Luckily, even on hot summer days when it becomes especially strong, it has not affected business.</p><p>"I guess we've just learned to kind of live with it," he said. "But it's very unpleasant."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-bd0000" "I would like to be informed on what measures are being taken to protect the residents of the community and what we need to be prepared for."</p><p>The MWRD did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The Thornton Reservoir is one of three reservoirs that make up the region's Deep Tunnel system, a network of more than 100 miles of underground tunnels designed to capture stormwater and reduce flooding across Chicago and surrounding suburbs. Combined with the McCook Reservoir, the system is currently holding roughly 11 billion gallons of water after weeks of persistent rainfall.</p><p>According to MWRD, water stored in the Thornton Reservoir is pumped to the Calumet Water Reclamation Plant, where it is treated before being returned to local waterways.</p><p>With additional rain in the forecast, nearby residents and businesses say they hope the water filling the reservoir subsides soon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" data-align-center> <a class="AnchorLink" id="gallery-a10001" name="gallery-a10001"></a> <div> <div class="Carousel-slides"> <div class="Carousel-slide"> <div class="CarouselSlide" > <div class="CarouselSlide-media"> <picture data-crop="large"> <source type="image/webp" width="840" height="555" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7b9ee3a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3615+0+16/resize/840x555!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4a%2F0e%2Fa9cbf7784eb0b826287787207f6e%2Fthorntonquarrysmell-260710-12.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d887b13/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3615+0+16/resize/1680x1110!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4a%2F0e%2Fa9cbf7784eb0b826287787207f6e%2Fthorntonquarrysmell-260710-12.jpg 2x"/> <source width="840" height="555" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/03046d8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3615+0+16/resize/840x555!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4a%2F0e%2Fa9cbf7784eb0b826287787207f6e%2Fthorntonquarrysmell-260710-12.jpg"/> <img class="Image" alt="Aerial view of the Thornton Reservoir in South Holland, Ill. entries.title: Chicago taxpayers on the hook for $9M wrongful conviction settlement
entries.summary: <p>Chicago taxpayers will spend $9 million to compensate a Spanish-speaking man who spent 17 years in prison after he was beaten and coerced as a teen into signing a confession for a murder he did not commit.</p><p>The latest in a seemingly never-ending string of wrongful conviction settlements tied to misconduct by Chicago Police officers — $131.5 million during the first six months alone, according to a WTTW analysis — goes to Alberto Ochoa.</p><p>Ochoa was a 17-year-old day laborer who had arrived in Chicago from Mexico less than a year before when he was arrested and charged with the December, 2002 murder of Marilu Sochu after being falsely identified by a known member of the Latin Kings street gang.</p><p>Chicago police officers, led by Jose “Pepe” Lopez, were accused of coercing one of several members of the Latin Kings arrested for a robbery that same night into identifying Ochoa as the killer of the girlfriend of a rival gang member. The gang members were "falsely" promised their immediate release if they identified the shooter.</p><p>Ochoa knew and worked with one of the Latin King members, who had come to Ochoa’s Little Village apartment the night of the murder to collect borrowed money.</p><p>But he was not a gang member and played no role in either the robbery or the murder of the young woman. Ochoa spent the night of the murder watching movies and drinking beer at home.</p><p>Attorney Jennifer Bonjean, who represented Ochoa, said the police misconduct that culminated in her client’s wrongful conviction follows a troubling and familiar pattern.</p><p>After being falsely implicated by that Latin King member and arrested by police, Bonjean said Ochoa was brutally abused and tricked into signing his name on a “fabricated” confession written only in English.</p><p>“He choked him and stuck his thumb deeply inside his sternal notch. It’s that little divot in your throat where the esophagus is. For months, he had to get medical treatment at Cermak [Hospital]. He was punched. He was struck. And he was hit in the genitals,” Bonjean said.</p><p>Before signing the ”fabricated” confession written in English, Bonjean said Ochoa asked to make a video-recorded statement instead. The request was denied, even though video recording equipment was available, she said.</p><p>“My client ended up signing — or really printing — his name on a handwritten statement that he could not read and did not write … implicating himself in this crime. There were statements in there that were completely fabricated, but he was none the wiser because he couldn’t read it,” Bonjean said Thursday.</p><p>“It is absolutely outrageous that you would have the lead detective on a case serving as both interpreter and lead detective with a non-English speaker. We can’t live in a world where people are signing … statements they can’t read. That was an outrageous act of misconduct,” she said.</p><p>“Lopez, this Spanish-speaking detective who was the only person he was communicating with, said, 'We just need you to make a statement, then you can go home.' The detective wrote out the statement in English, even though a video recording was available, and my client asked for his statement to be video-recorded. It was denied. So, he essentially signed a statement that implicated himself that he couldn’t read. And there were aspects of it that Detective Lopez had fabricated.”</p><p>Ochoa, who is now working as a truck driver, was released from prison in October 2019. He was granted a certificate of innocence in November 2023.</p><p>The City Council’s Finance Committee will be asked to approve the $9 million settlement during Monday’s meeting.</p><p>Also on the agenda is the proposal by New York investment firm Stonepeak Partners to acquire Chicago parking meters for $2.53 billion — $800 million more than the bid submitted, then abandoned by Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>Ald. Andre Vasquez (40th) chair of the Hispanic Caucus, said he “couldn’t in good conscience” support the acquisition because of the controversy created by Stonepeak’s 2025 acquisition of Omni Air International, which has provided “long haul” deportation flights for the Department of Homeland Security.</p><p>Vasquez was not satisfied by Stonepeak’s pledge to consider selling Omni.</p><p>“Considering is one thing. Actually doing it is another,” Vasquez said.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson has denied playing hide the ball with a City Council that must decide whether to approve the sale by July 24.</p><p>Finance Committee Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) doesn't buy it.</p><p>"We have not received all of the information that we requested from the administration. They claim that they have a non-disclosure confidentiality requirement. That's not true," she said.</p><p>Dowell said she intends to call for a vote Monday, and "anything can happen" between now and then.</p>

entries.title: Trader Joe's in North Center nabs union win after two-year ordeal
entries.summary: <p>A North Center Trader Joe's became the first unionized location in Illinois, more than two years after employees cast votes to join the union.</p><p>The grocery store, at 3745 N. Lincoln Ave., will become the fifth in the country to join the Trader Joe’s United independent union. </p><p>“For the Chicago crew … [this is] an example of how grit and constant fighting can lead to these results, despite the fact of how much money Trader Joe's has and how much appeal power they claim to wield,” Trader Joe’s United National President Roberts Hönisch said. “So what we see right now in Chicago is an example that the workers aren't done with this. It wasn't a fleeting idea.”</p><p>The employees voted 70-70 in April 2024, with Trader Joe’s contesting one additional vote in the election, arguing it was cast by an employee ineligible to vote. The company said the worker was a temporary transfer to the store, but union supporters said it was a permanent transfer, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2024/11/01/trader-joes-union/" target="_blank" >Chicago Tribune</a> reported.</p><p>Trader Joe’s took its case to the National Labor Relations Board, also alleging interference by union supporters in the election. When the board voted in favor of Trader Joe’s United, the company appealed the decision.</p><p>The worker's vote was in favor of the union, bringing the tally to 71-70 when the challenged vote was opened Wednesday.</p><p>Trader Joe's didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Trader Joe’s United formed in 2022, with the first union store in Hadley, Massachusetts, followed by stores in Minneapolis, Louisville, Kentucky, and Oakland, California.</p><p>The Lincoln Avenue store would have about 140 union members, Hönisch said. </p><p>Trader Joe’s United is still bargaining for its first contract.</p><p>The grocer has enjoyed a reputation for being progressive, but the union said behind the scenes, it has engaged in union busting and "surface-level bargaining." </p><p>“There is truthfully some scary stuff that you see going on on the national level with the company,” Hönisch said. “We often find that sometimes when talking to the national company, it seems almost like a complete pivot from the usual grocery store that you and I are both familiar with.”</p><p>He said management has said its locations don't need a union.</p><p>Over the years, the company has faced several other labor-related complaints, ranging from alleged retaliation against workers at a Massachusetts store during a 2022 union push, to firing a Texas employee concerned about COVID-19 safety protocols in 2022.</p><p>"Trader Joe's sort of operates in this area when they feel like they can get away with something, they'll attempt it,” Hönisch said. “However, it makes all of us question what values does the company truly stand for.”</p><p>Trader Joe’s has six locations in Chicago and more than 600 nationwide.</p>

entries.title: Red Sox keep White Sox' bats quiet to complete sweep
entries.summary: <p>Rate Field largely has been a haven for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> this season. They’ve played their best baseball there, ranking second in the American League with 28 victories.</p><p>This week, though, they’ve seemed to lack the energy they usually play with there. The Red Sox’ pitching had a lot to do with that.</p><p>In completing a three-game sweep Thursday with a 2-1 victory, the Red Sox held the White Sox to two runs and 15 hits in 27 innings — all singles — and struck them out 25 times.</p><p>“Same story today,” manager Will Venable said. “Just couldn’t solve for some really good left-handed pitching. Have to give those guys on the other side credit. They pitched us extremely tough. They were able to neutralize some guys that we’ve seen, especially against left-handed pitching, play really well.”</p><p>Patrick Sandoval, the Red Sox’ third left-handed starter of the series, made his first major-league start since June 21, 2024, after recovering from Tommy John surgery. He allowed one run and five hits in 4⅓ innings with one walk and five strikeouts. The Red Sox’ bullpen allowed two hits and zero walks the rest of the way. A one-run lead never felt so big.</p><p>“We’ve played really well at home for 10 series in a row,” said designated hitter Andrew Benintendi, who drove in the Sox’ run on a checked-swing tapper up the third-base line. “So it was bound to happen at some point, going through a rough stretch. Credit to them, they pitched really well.”</p><h3>Down on the farm</h3><p>If the Sox seek help for the bullpen later this season, they might find it in Triple-A Charlotte. Hard-throwing right-hander Tanner McDougal, who’s back with the Knights after recovering from a strained flexor, will pitch out of the bullpen for the rest of the season.</p><p>“Going into next year, we still would aspire for him to train in the offseason to build up as a starter,” Sox director of player development Paul Janish said of the club’s fifth-ranked prospect. “But for the purpose of impact on the major-league team this year, Tanner is going to be pitching out of the pen, with the ability to go multiple [innings], potentially pitch two out of three days.”</p><p>On Tuesday, McDougal made his first appearance for the Knights since April 29, striking out two in one inning. He has held hitters to a .145 batting average and has struck out 29 in 25 innings for Charlotte this season.</p><p>• Left-hander Hagen Smith, the Sox’ third-ranked prospect, was scheduled to throw his first side session Thursday on his way back from a shoulder impingement. Janish said all signs point to him returning to game action after the All-Star break.</p><p>• Sox Opening Day starter Shane Smith is building up to start again. The right-hander, who’s recovering from a strained rotator cuff, has thrown in two rehab outings at High-A Winston-Salem and should return to Charlotte soon, Janish said.</p><h3>Derby day is Saturday</h3><p>Former Sox outfielder Scott Podsednik arrived in town early for the Alumni Home Run Derby, which will follow the game Saturday. The leadoff man for the Sox’ 2005 World Series champions readily admitted his chances of winning are slim.</p><p>“I’m probably not one of the favorites,” said Podsednik, who had 42 homers in 11 big-league seasons. “I probably have the least amount of home runs of anyone to ever participate in a home-run derby. So I’ve got that going for me.”</p><p>The other participants are Gordon Beckham, Jose Canseco, Leury Garcia, Daniel Palka and Alexei Ramirez.</p><p>“I’ve hit three times in the cages off the tee,” he said. “I’m hoping just to provide a little bit of entertainment. I don’t know if I can get one out of the ballpark anymore.”</p><h3>Roster move</h3><p>The Sox put <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/09/chicago-white-sox-put-reliever-trevor-richards-on-family-emergency-list-recall-tyler-davis" >right-handed reliever Trevor Richards</a> on the bereavement/family medical-emergency list and recalled right-hander Tyler Davis from Charlotte. Richards has been pitching well of late, posting a 1.37 ERA in his last 18 outings (four earned runs in 26⅓ innings).</p><h3>ON DECK</h3><p><b>ATHLETICS AT SO</b>X</p><p><b>Friday:</b> TBA vs. Sean Burke (5-4, 3.56 ERA), 6:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p><b>Saturday:</b> Gage Jump (3-3, 3.77) vs. Erick Fedde (4-6, 4.34), 1:10 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p><b>Sunday:</b> J.T. entries.title: 16-year-old charged as second suspect in 2024 Chatham quadruple shooting that killed 14-year-old, 2 others
entries.summary: <p>Cynthia Jones, grandmother of Amere Deese, treasures her years-old voice recording of her grandson from his eighth grade graduation.</p><p>"Sometimes I have to sit and listen to his voice, even if it’s just 40 seconds," Jones told the Chicago Sun-Times Thursday.</p><p>Hours earlier, nearly 2½ years after Amere, then 14, was shot and killed, a 16-year-old was charged in the killing, according to Chicago police. That teen is the second suspect charged in the Feb. 25, 2024, shooting in Chatham that also claimed two other lives.</p><p>The teen charged Thursday faces three counts of first-degree murder, along with six other related murder charges, as well as a count of attempted murder and a charge of armed robbery, police said. He was arrested Wednesday in the 6700 block of South Loomis Boulevard.</p><p>The other suspect, Antonio Velasco, then 16, was arrested in Hazel Crest and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/03/21/boy-16-charged-with-killing-three-in-chatham-shooting-including-14-year-old" target="_blank" ><u>charged as an adult in March 2024</u></a> in connection with the homicides, police said. He was hit with 43 charges, including first-degree murder, attempted robbery and aggravated battery.</p><p>Prosecutors and family members said Velasco had been like an older brother to Deese, but he opened fire in the home after deciding he wanted to steal a rifle, prosecutors said. </p><p>Jones said the charges brought her family a sense of relief. They'd been cautious since the shooting, considering that one of the suspects was still on the loose. She said the teen charged Thursday attended a nearby school, and her other grandson was moved to a school in another neighborhood to avoid any possible interaction.</p><p>Jones said after Amere's mom died of cirrhosis of the liver two years before his shooting, his family had tried to make sure he was well taken care of. Amere also would give out any extra clothes or shoes he had to friends, including Velasco and the 16-year-old charged Thursday.</p><p>“To know somebody hurt him in this way that he shared so much with, it’s just very hurtful,” Jones told the Sun-Times Thursday afternoon. "I don't understand it."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-850000" Velasco returned to the room with a handgun and opened fire, they said.</p><p>The hail of bullets killed Deese; Ladeverett West-Ringgold, 20; and Randy Graham, 36. A 16-year-old boy also in the room was wounded.</p><p>Deese had still been reeling from his mother's death, but was on a better path, his grandmother said.</p><p>Jones remembered her grandson as a "funny young man," always willing to break into a silly dance if he knew it would make his sisters laugh when they were sad. Now she is quick to do the same when his sisters miss him.</p><p>“We were so happy when he decided to straighten up. He was 'Mr. School,' doing everything he needed to do in life for himself,” Jones said. “We’re still in the grieving process; it hurts."</p><p>A hearing has not been set for the 16-year-old charged, according to Cook County court records. Velasco’s case is ongoing; the next court date in that case is set for July 23.</p><p>“I feel bad for everybody in this situation, including these two young men who did this," Jones said. entries.title: No real All-Star break for Alex Bregman? Cubs know third baseman will be itching to get back to work
entries.summary: <p>BALTIMORE — <b>Alex Bregman</b> had to chuckle.</p><p>With Bregman starting to feel a lot more like himself at the plate, Orioles first baseman <b>Pete Alonso</b> offered a reminder this week that the recent warm-up is coming at the same time as the All-Star break.</p><p>“Perfect,” Bregman recalled sarcastically responding.</p><p>But a break is not a break, apparently, when you’re the Cubs’ third baseman.</p><p>“He’ll be obsessed with it the four days we’re not playing, I can assure you that,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said with a laugh Thursday. “That’s just who he’s going to be. He’ll have his helmet on six hitters before he’s ready to hit. That’s just who he is. That’s not going to change. He’s going to be sending people videos during the break, that’s just who he is.</p><p>“That’s what he’s going to do. That’s how he finds answers.”</p><p>The big-money free-agent addition has earned a reputation for being a hard worker behind the scenes, even as his production hasn’t been where he has wanted it to be.</p><p>Things are going better for Bregman of late, perhaps more so visibly than statistically.</p><p>He’s 60 percent of the way to matching the number of extra-base hits he had in June just seven games into July. But it was Bregman hitting the ball harder on an oh-fer day at the plate Wednesday that had Counsell raving, calling it “maybe one of his best days.”</p><p>Getting back to the Bregman version of normalcy? That means continuing to work, even as the rest of the sport takes a midsummer break.</p><p>“He’s been a worker, always putting in the time, really putting a lot of time in on his craft,” first baseman <b>Michael Busch</b> said. “Even when he was scuffling a little bit, as some would say, in my eyes he was still having really good at-bats, putting the ball in play, still getting on base. And now you’re seeing some of those balls maybe hit a little harder, more line drives.</p><p>“The focus on the craft every day has been pretty special.”</p><h3><b>Peterson’s mixed bag</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Lefty starter <b>David Peterson</b> bounced back from allowing 10 runs in a woeful second outing as a Cub to keep the Orioles to just a run in Thursday’s 3-2 loss.</p><p>Results were still mixed. The ground-ball specialist walked four batters and allowed a homer in his third straight start since being acquired from the Mets. But the Cubs saw positives, too, beyond the minimal damage on the scoreboard.</p><p>“It was, obviously, better than his last start,” Counsell said. “There’s still some inconsistencies there, but I also thought he showed the really good version of himself, too.</p><p>“It’s not going to happen overnight, but we took some steps today, hopefully. We’ve just got to work on getting more consistent. Certainly a good outing, and he got the job done.”</p><h3><b>Backstop bats</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Cubs catchers have once again been some of baseball’s best with the bat, waking up Thursday with the position’s best on-base percentage in baseball.</p><p>Mostly due to the work of <b>Carson Kelly</b> and <b>Miguel Amaya</b> (though <b>Moises Ballesteros</b> has also played eight games at catcher this season), Cubs backstops were reaching base at an eye-popping .370 clip, with a .264 batting average only two points off the league lead.</p><p>It was enough for a wRC-plus of 118, making the Cubs’ catching corps the second most productive in the sport, behind only the Twins.</p><p>“Our catchers, in general, have quietly, again, provided really good production,” Counsell said. “Last year, it was a bunch of home runs. This year, the best part has been their on-base [percentage]. They’ve just done a great job of getting on base.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Johnson's advisory referendum on millionaires tax shot down in latest Council rebellion
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson's bid to pressure the Illinois General Assembly to pass a tax on millionaires by putting an advisory referendum on the Chicago ballot was shot down Thursday in the latest act of defiance by an already emboldened City Council.</p><p>Johnson waited until the last Rules Committee meeting before the August recess to introduce the millionaires tax referendum directly to committee.</p><p>But members of the rebel bloc that rejected Johnson's corporate head tax before approving an alternative city budget refused to go along with the mayor's 11th-hour maneuver.</p><p>They argued that Roberts Rules of Order, which govern City Council proceedings, requires that direct introductions to committee be reserved for emergencies, and an advisory referendum simply doesn't qualify.</p><p>It was retiring Ald. Marty Quinn (13th) who led the charge to checkmate Johnson.</p><p>He accused the mayor of attempting to run roughshod over Council rules simply because he “can’t get his act together” before the late August deadline to place advisory questions on the November ballot.</p><p>“The fact that the mayor is going to do a direct introduction under the disguise of an emergency on a non-binding referendum? No. I’m gonna call b.s. on that, and I did. And I won,” Quinn told the Sun-Times after the meeting.</p><p>“It has less to do with the subject matter and more to do with the pattern of abuse. We have to stand up against that because that’s gonna continue. You can’t do that. You have to push back on it. This is part of being co-equal," he said. "We all have rules. We have to follow the same rules. It’s can’t be one set of rules for the mayor and another set of rules for the Council. That can’t happen.”</p><p>Ald. Scott Waguespack (32nd) served as Finance Committee chair under now-former Mayor Lori Lightfoot before being deposed by Johnson.</p><p>Waguespack noted that, even during the genuine emergency created by the pandemic, “only a certain type” of direct mayoral introductions “were allowed to move forward.”</p><p>“I’m a little perplexed about why we keep getting to this point because it is a violation of our rules, and it needs to stop,” Waguespack said.</p><p>“It will allow the 5th floor — whether it’s in this term with this mayor or future mayors — to essentially break the rules of the City Council," he said. "This is about the rules. And if we’re just going to sit here and let the 5<sup>th</sup> floor break them, what’s the point of being here?"</p><p>Ald. Ray Lopez (15th) added: “This is political theater. This is garbage.”</p><p>Johnson has repeatedly gone around Roberts Rules of Order, which require non-emergency items to be introduced to the full Council, then referred to the appropriate committee.</p><p>The mayor used a direct introduction to committee to speed consideration of the Renter Protection Ordinance he hopes to use to court renters, a potentially potent voting bloc that includes roughly 660,000 Chicago voters.</p><p>After thwarting Johnson, the Rules Committee approved four alternative questions — one of them another direct introduction from Johnson — forcing the full Council to choose three out of those four, since city election law includes a three-question limit.</p><p>Alderpersons made an exception for that one mayoral introduction because of the politically volatile subject matter.</p><p>It asks voters whether Chicago should “pursue all lawful means" to recover financial compensation from the federal government for the costs and economic harm caused by the federal immigration raids known as Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>That one will compete for a spot on the November ballot with three other advisory questions submitted by the same renegade bloc.</p><p>One would ask whether Chicago should “restart the use of gunshot detection technology that informs first responders when gunshots are detected." Another asks if Chicago should make its “contribution to city pension funds in the first quarter of the year to reduce long-term debt.” And the third asks voters whether Chicago should develop a "permanent festival and outdoor event space” for large-scale gatherings.</p><p>Chicago mayors and their City Council allies have a long history of using the three-referendums-per-election limit to their advantage.</p><p>They routinely put innocuous referendums on the ballot to crowd out other, more controversial questions that would have risked bolstering turnout among already ornery voters who might vent their anger against incumbents.</p><p>The mayor's office pushed back hard against the latest in a string of Council rebellions.</p><p>"The same members who chose to sic debt collectors on working Chicagoans instead of taxing the largest corporations, plunging us into a $130 million budget hole with an alternative budget based on faulty projections, have yet again gone out of their way to stand in the way of a progressive revenue that would enable consistent, reliable funding for our public schools and the critical services Chicagoans rely on every day," the mayor's office statement said.</p><p></p><p>"This begs the question: Do they believe in taxing the wealthy at all? Instead, they chose to deny Chicagoans a voice, reviving Machine-era traditions of keeping the public out of decisions that directly affect their lives in lieu of ballot questions that are moot and do nothing to address the real challenges our residents face."</p><p></p><p>The mayor's office also noted "70% of Chicago voters" supported Gov. JB Pritzker's failed binding referendum that would have paved the way for a graduated income tax in Illinois.</p><p>"Rather than trust voters to weigh in again, these members chose to shield powerful special interests instead of standing with working people," the mayor's statement said.</p>
